Mr. Speaker, by your leave I would call the attention of the House to a matter which in my judgment concerns and deeply affects the privileges of this House. I refer to an incident which took place some few days ago when the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) was addressing the House during the Budget debate. My hon. friend from St. John referred to a statement which had been made by Professor Shortt as to the number of dismissals and appointments under the present Administration, to which statement very strong exception was at once taken by the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers). Perhaps in order that the House may be seized of the tenor of the incident, I had better read what took place. The hon. member from St. John said:
I have not that familiarity with the Civil Service that Professor Shortt, chairman of the Civil Service Commission, necessarily has. He is a gentleman who is in the employ of the Government; he occupies, X presume, a quasi independent position as chairman of that commission ; he has made the statement, made it publicly, made it with deliberation that under this Government the appointments to the Civil Service in the lower grades are entirely a matter of patronage and he says that, whereas there have been something like 2,000 dismissals from the Civil Sendee, there have been some 10,000 appointments, making a difference of some S,000.
The hon. member for St. John was interrupted by the Minister of Public Works in these words:
I would like to say that this is a statement that has been repeated so often in this House that hon. gentlemen opposite will possibly be beginning to believe it. No more dishonourable, no more dishonest, no more unfair-

Then there was some confusion and interruption and the Ihon. minister proceeded:
I have repeated it twice, but I shall be glad to stay here and go on repeating it if it will be any benefit to my hon. friend. I was referring not to my hon. friend but to Professor Shortt and in 'that connection X want to say here and now that no more dishonourable, no more dishonest, no more unfair statement was ever made by any man than that made by Professor Shortt, chairman of the Civil Service Commission. It is an absolutely untrue statement.
These, Mr. Speaker, are very strong words, as I am sure that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works will be the first to admit. To charge a man in the position of Professor Shortt with being guilty of dishonourable and dishonest conduct is as grave a charge as can be made against any man. Professor Shortt occupies not only an official position in Canada, but I may say that he also occupies a very high position otherwise. He is chairman of the Civil Service Commission, and in that respect is amenable and responsible notQo the Government but to the two Houses of Parliament. He is appointed under section 9 of the Civil Service Act of 1908, which enacts:
There shall be a commission, to be called the Civil Service Commission, consisting of two members appointed by the Governor in Council.
2. The rank, standing and salary of each commissioner shall be those of a deputy head of a department; and each commissioner shall hold office during good behaviour, but shall be removable by the Governor General on address of the Senate and House of Commons.
These words in the .statute are the basis upon which I claim that the House has jurisdiction and ought to take cognizance of such a charge as is now upon the head of Professor Shortt. If an officer of this Parliament or of this country, a public servant in the capacity and of the character of Professor Shortt should be attacked by a Minister of the Crown as having made a dishonest and untrue and dishonourable statement, everybody will agree that the usefulness of the chairman of the Civil Service Commission would be very much impaired, to say the least. Professor Shortt's attention was called to the words of the minister, and in an interview which he. gave the following day, the 26th of February, in the Free Press, he expressed himself as follows:
"I have only this to say," replied Dr. Shortt, " The official return is there to speak for itself. It is dated March of last year.' I was simply quoting from the return, and I have nothing to do with whatever interpretation Mr. Rogers or Dr. Pugsley may place on that re-

turn. I had no information other than was contained in the return-for instance, I had no information about resignations.
" I made the statement that there had been two thousand odd dismissed and ten thousand odd appointed, not including the Post Office Department, merely incidental to a discussion of the outside service. Only two dismissals were reported in the inside service. I pointed out that this was not a matter of party politics so far as I was concerned. My remarks as reported were correct in substance.
I repeat, they were founded solely on the information contained in the return and nothing else."
It does not seem clear to me-and I would toe glad to have the explanation of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works upon this point, as to what was the particular statement made by Professor Shortt in this connection to which the minister takes exception. Hr. Shortt made two statements, viz., that there had been 2,000 dismissals and 10,000 appointments. I do not know and I would be glad to know from the Minister of Public Works whether he impugned the statement as to the 2,000 dismissals or as to the 10,000 appointments, or both. If I may be permitted to speak frankly to my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works,
I would say that there has been something almost like quibbling over these dismissals; for later on in the debate the Minister of Public Works, addressing himself to the hon. member for St. John, spoke as follows:
He has surely not read the return himself or he would not venture to make that statement. The return shows nothing of the kind. Take the return of my own department for instance; in it 507 dismissals are credited and there are 700 odd resignations which Professor Shortt never takes into account.
I say with all candour to my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works that 1 should be glad to be enlightened as to these resignations. Five hundred dismissals is a pretty good number, and seven hundred resignations seems to be a more goodly number. Resignation is a virtue we know, but there is such a thing as being virtuous under compulsion. I have not found in the course of my experience that the spirit of resignation in our time is so prevalent as to lead to seven hundred resignations in one department. The point, however is not whether these resignations were voluntary or not. I shall be very glad to take the word of my hon. friend upon that. But the point of the charge made by the hon. member for St. John was that there have been two thousand vacancies-whether those vacancies were caused by resignation or by dismissals-and ten thousand appointments.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It seems to me that
inconvenience may arise from the manner in which this matter is being brought before the House. I did not understand the right hon. gentleman to say that he was bringing it before the House strictly as a question of privilege. I take it that a discussion such as is now taking place should be based on a motion of some kind. It could hardly be brought before the House properly as a question of privilege.
I brought the matter up solely as a question of privilege.

I am quite willing to
hear the right hon. gentleman, but I submit that this is not a question of privilege. It does not come within that category.

If Professor
Shortt was a member of the Civil Service he would be strictly amenable to the jurisdiction of the Government alone; and the House would have no control over him. But Professor Shortt is not an officer of the Government. The Government cannot remove him; they cannot control him; they cannot give him any orders. The only body which has any authority over Professor Shortt is the Parliament of Canada, the House of Commons and the Senate. If this be correct, then in my judgment this discussion comes within the privileges of this House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not desire to prevent my right hon. friend from having the fullest opportunity of discussing this question. I do not understand, however, that he can go into some of the matters which he introduced into the later part of his remarks as a question of privilege, namely, the discussion of how many dismissals and resignations there have been. But I am perfectly willing now to move the House into Committee of Supply in order to give my right hon. friend and other hon. gentlemen the fullest opportunity of discussing this matter.
On the motion of Sir Robert Borden for Committee of Supply:

I was going to say that on this occasion I did not intend to discuss the number of dismissals or resignations. I am not in a position to do so, for I have never seen the return. I asked the Clerk of -the House for the report, and I only got a partial one. I have never seen the complete report. The point to which I wish to call the attention of the

House is this: A public officer of this country, occupying under the law of the land a most important position and daily fulfilling the functions of that office, has 'been charged with conduct which has been characterized as dishonourable and dishonest. My point is this: Should an officer of this kind remain under the imputation that has been made against him without being given an opportunity to repel the charge ? That is the only reason I have brought the matter before the House. My point is that the language of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works was so strong against that public officer, that he owes it to himself either to be more precise or to give Professor Shortt an opportunity to defend himself. That is the only thing I wish for. Professor Shortt has been impugned in violent language by the Minister of Public Works, and it is not fair that an officer of his importance should remain under that imputation. Professor Shortt staked his reputation on the statement he made. That statement may be true or not, but I say that Professor Shortt should be given an opportunity to vindicate his own words. After the Minister of Public Works has made such a violent charge against Professor Shortt as to say that he was dishonest and dishonourable, I say it is only fair that Professor Shortt should be given an opportunity to defend himself, and that this matter should be investigated. That is the only reason for my action to-day. As to the question of dismissals, we can deal with that later. I appeal to the spirit of fairness of the Prime Minister, and of the whole House, that an opportunity be given to have this matter investigated, and the responsibility placed where it belongs. If Professor Shortt has made a dishonest and dishonourable statement he is liable to the heaviest censure of this House; and if the language of the Minister of Public Works was not called for, then some justice must be done to the man who was attacked.

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (Minister oi Public Works):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say at once that I hope I would he the last man in this House who would venture to make any statement, implied or otherwise, upon any occasion, at any time, or under any circumstances, that I did not honestly and fairly feel I was justified in making. My right hon. friend suggests that the remarks I made upon the occasion to which he has referred affect the privileges of this House.
I made the statement which I did, conscious of the knowledge of the circumstances ces, believing that I was right, and believing 
that I was justified in making that statement. I would not desire to be guilty of making a statement against Professor Shortt or against the most humble citizen of this . Dominion of Canada that I did not believe I was justified in making. If my right hon. friend is willing to accept the statement of Professor Shortt, and to accept blame and condemnation at the hands of that gentleman, similar to the charge which Professor Shortt presumed to make against hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, why then let him take that responsibility. If my right hon. friend is willing to accept that position, and stand up here before Parliament and the country and commend Professor Shortt for such a statement, then my right hon. friend must settle it with his own friends on that side of the House, because when Professor Shortt made the statement which had been quoted by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), and to which I took exception the other night, he immediately weht on to say:
What he had said hits one party no more than the other.
If hon. gentlemen are willing to accept such a statement as that from Professor Shortt, and to take the responsibility for it, all I can say is that we on this side of the House do not propose to accept any such statement from Professor Shortt. My right hon. friend has quoted the statement made by Professor Shortt, following the reference to him in the House on Thursday evening last, and he has quoted correctly, I believe, from the Free Press what Professor Shortt had to say. Let me read these words because I think they are of importance:
" I have only this to say," replied Dr. Shortt.
" The official return is there to speak for itself." It is dated March of last year. I was simply quoting from the return, and I have nothing to do with whatever interpretation Mr. Rogers or Dr. Pugsley may place on that return. I had no information other than was contained in the return-for instance, I had no information about resignations.
My right hon. friend was careful to say that he had not studied the returns. These returns were laid upon the table of the House from every department of the Government and it is evident from Professor Shortt's statement that he had such returns. They were simple answers to very simple questions. The questions were:
1.	How many employees if the Federal Government of Canada, including all services and all departments, have been dismissed from October 10, 1911 to the present date.
2.	How many have resigned?

3.	How many have deserted the service?
4.	How many deserters have been punished?
5.	How many new employees have been engaged or appointed by the present Government during the same period?
The answers are as follows from my particular department, and I am dealing only with the Department of Public Works for the moment:
1.	Dismissals 511.
2.	Resignations, 725.
3.	None.
4.	None.
5.	1877.
Professor Shortt acknowledged that he only had the return before him. If he had that return before him he had from the Department of Public Works a return showing that 725 resignations had taken place, and I am sure that my right hon. friend, during the fifteen years that he was in office never had a resignation that he did not have to fill the vacancy. No one knew or understood this better than did Professor Shortt. No one had a better knowledge of the facts and if you take all the resignations in the various departments, which were under the hand of Professor Shortt when he studied that report, you will find that there are very nearly 4,000 resignations to be taken from that 10,000 referred to by Professor Shortt. Was I not, therefore, justified in characterising the mischievous statement of Professor Shortt in the language I did in view of the fact that we have from day to day, not alone in this House, but outside of it, statements being made based upon the authority of the statement made by Professor Shortt with respect to a return that he misquoted unfairly. Not only that, but in view of his statement made the following day in the Free Press, I will go a step further and say that Professor Shortt's statement was not only dishonourable and dishonest but, according to his own statement, it is untrue, because he said there was nothing in the report in respect to resignations.
These are the circumstances which led to the language of which my right hon. friend complained and while it may have been strong I felt that it was justified. I felt that it was justified by reason of the fact that hon. gentlemen upon the other side of the House were referring to it and taking advantage of Professor Shortt's statement to have it circulated throughout the length and breadth of the country, that the Government had dismissed 2,000 officials and had replaced them with 10,000. Surely my right hon. friend, in view of the circumstances, will admit that this was a very unfair statement on the part of Professor Shortt because he admits himself in his interview that he had under his hand a copy of the return. That being so I say it was very unfair for him to make that statement and to place before this country a statement that is not borne out by the facts. I think it was the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) who first used these figures in the House. He was followed by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) and it was only when the statements were repeated by an hon. member with a knowledge of the conditions such as my hon. friend from St. John always has, that I thought it was time that we should correct the misstatements that were being circulated throughout the length and breadth of the country as coming from Professor Shortt. Not only did we have this statement made in this House, but we were having this, statement of Professor Shortt's circulated in all parts of the Dominions My hon. friend the member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), a few days previously, called to task hon. members on this side of the House for being guilty of keeping open the information bureau of the Conservative party in the city of Ottawa. He used rather strong language upon that occasion and was rather severe in his condemnation. Perhaps he will pardon me if I quote a few of the words that he was good enough to use:
From the moment that war broke out the bureau was closed.
Referring to the Liberal bureau.
So far as I am concerned, I have never seen a document emanate from it since that time, of a petty nature or of any other nature. Where is the laugh of my hon. friends now? Can they produce a leaflet or a document? Not a single one. And I should be wanting in common manliness if I did not assert it.
My hon. friend from Red Deer, as we all well know, lives only in the shade of Cob-den and of Bright and he is evidently not aware that a very large portion of the Liberal party in the Dominion of Canada are getting their monthly leaflets to-day just the same as they were before the war started. It is to this particular little Liberal monthly I wish to draw the attention of the House to now. It was issued only a few days ago, on February 15, and I have a bundle of these leaflets here for the benefit of my hon. friend from Red Deer. This little bulletin for February undertakes to quote the same figures as did Professor Shortt. The article reads as follows:

Return tabled in the House of Commons February 12, giving statement as to dismissals and appointments in the Civil Service since the Government came Into power in 1911 makes almost incredible reading, and throws into "vivid light the extent to which the party axe has been wielded and how the influence of patronage has been invoked under the Conservative Administration. The return is admittedly not complete and was made up from the different departments on varying dates since the spring of 1911. Yet it shows a record of no less than 2,000 dismissals and 10,576 new appointments.
Such statements, emanating from the Liberal bureau and bearing upon the statement of Professor Shortt in respect to the matter under discussion, are being circulated broadcast. It is true that Professor Shortt went a little farther in that famous speech of his, in which he made that statement, and he went on to tell of an individual who had spoken to him about how rotten the patronage system was in the Dominion of Canada. Since I came here hundreds of people have spoken to me of how rotten the patronage system is in the city of Ottawa, but almost invariably those people have pointed to Professor Shortt as a living example of the abuse of the administration of patronage.
As regards my department, I have nothing to hide in respect to the return. In the outside service we have to account for 1,877 appointments, and as there were 511 dismissals and 722 resignations we, therefore, have to account for having made 669 new appointments during the three years covered by this return.
What about the 25 inside service appointments in the Department of Public Works?

I will come to the inside service later on. I am giving the outside service first, so that the matter will be understood by hon. members in all its details.
In the Chief Architect's branch, according to the return, we have to account for an increase of 244. In that branch of the Department we have had under the progressive administration of the present Government erected during the three years that we have been in office something over seventy new public buildings in various parts of the Dominion. Some of these require one or more caretaker's, and others as many as six where there are elevators and furnaces to look after. Therefore the increase of 244 in the Chief Architect's branch is accounted for by the increase in the number of public buildings erected in the various parts of the Dominion.
[Mr. Rogers.
On the staff of the Superintendent of Dominion Buildings we have an increase to account for of 99. This increase is rendered necessary on account of the engineers, firemen, watchmen and elevator men required for the buildings rented and occupied as Government offices, the new Mines Building, and the addition to the West Block. There is also the general staff of labourers and artisans required in connection with the general maintenance of buildings.
In the chief engineer's branch we have to account for an increase of 100, and this is accounted for by the addition of assistant engineers to the staffs of the 36 district engineers throughout the Dominion, rendered necessary by the increased number of harbour works during the past three years.
The expenditure of the chief en-4 p.m. gineer's branch in 1911 was about $3,200,000, and in 1914, $7,700,000. That shows the necessity for the increased staff for carrying out the additional work.
The increase of 157 in the assistant chief engineer's branch, which has to do with the dredging operations of the department, is accounted for by the manning of new departmental plant, by the large British Columbia dredges having been put on double shift, and the natural increases in the crews of the various dredges and tugs throughout the Dominion to cope with the increased dredging operations. On account of the British Columbia dredges working a double shift, we have been obliged to add 100 employees. That accounts for 100 out of. the total increase of 157. The department has no-w seven more tugs than it had in 1911. The expenditure for 1911 was $5,030,000, and in 1914, $6,200,000.
The increase of 69 in the telegraph staff is accounted for by the increased mileage of telegraph lines and the number of new offices opened since October 10, 1911. In 1911, the mileage was 8,639|, and in 1914, 10,312, or an increase of 1,672|. The number of offices in 1911 was 624, and in 1914, 671, or an increase of 47. The provision of operators for these offices and the line repairers for the additional . mileage accounts for the increase in staff. The same answer applies exactly in the case of the inside service.
As regards the inside service in the chief architect's branch, I would like to call the attention of the House to the fact that in 1911 the expenditure for public buildings was $4,150,000, and in 1914, $12,400,000. That shows the necessity for appointing an

additional number of architects and draughtmen and the same thing applies to the other branches of the department over which it is my privilege to preside.
To what date is the return brought down?

I have not yet been able to see the return, for the simple reason that I have several times asked the Clerk of the House for it, but I have always been informed that it is in the hands of Liberal members who have been giving it very close consideration. I hold in my hand a return of my own department.
To what date is that return brought down?
It does not give the date. Professor Shortt gives the date as March, 1914. I do not know whether he is correct or not; I would not like to say that he is.
Will the returns of all the departments be given to us before we proceed with the discussion of this motion?
No.
My hon. friend will see how very inconvenient it would be to have a proper discussion of the question without the return, and without knowing the dates to which they were brought down.

I have not given any consideration to that. I do not know anything about the return, not having been able to see it myself. I am only dealing with the facts as I find them. I complain of the circulation of a mis-statement which is being used for political purposes against the Government of the day, a mis-statement which neither Professor Shortt nor any other man is justified in making as against the present Administration. If we have had increases in the service, they have been due to the development of our country, and we have had only such increases as were necessary for the public service. I wish to express my surprise, and regret, that my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) should allow his little paper from the Liberal Bureau to circulate a statement of this sort and send it broadcast throughout the country. I would like, on behalf of my good friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark), to express my, surprise that he has not been kept better informed as to what is going on at the Liberal headquarters. I hold in my hand a letter from a Mr. Godard, dated 26th February, attached to a circular in which he is making an appeal, and he uses this language:
Can you afford to be without this publication? The Canadian Liberal Monthly is published each month at the Central Liberal Information Office at Ottawa. It Is prepared under the personal supervision and direction of the Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should be very sorry indeed, let me say again, to use one syllable that could be regarded as harsh or unfair as against any individual m discussing any public question. At the same time, as a member of this Government, I do not propose to stand for mis-statements from Professor Shortt or anybody else. The documents and returns are placed freely on the table of this House for the benefit of hon. gentlemen opposite. I do not think these hon. gentlemen have anything to complain of in that regard and so far as I am concerned, they are at all times welcome to all the information it is possible to give them. At the same time, I hope that in future there will be no misrepresentations either by Professor Shortt or by anybody else with respect to returns that we lay upon the table of this House.

I desire to ask the Minister of Public Works if his position is that Professor Shortt is incorrect in stating that the increase in the appointments numbered 8,000? What Professor Shortt said was that ten thousand had been appointed and two thousand dismissed, giving an increase in the service of eight thousand. Does the minister controvert that statement that there was an increase of eight thousand in the service?

That is where my hon.
friend goes wrong. I had hoped that I had made myself so clear that even my hon. friend would understand me. I said there were two thousand dismissals and four-thousand resignations, a total of six thousand, and therefore the Government have to account to Parliament and to the people for an increase in the service of something like four thousand' according to these figures. I have accounted for an increase in my own department of 669.

I took the trouble to
examine this report about which there has been so much controversy in the House, and I made a table showing the exact figures contained in it, with the exception of the Mounted Police. I did not think it was fair to charge the Government with appointments to the Mounted Police, so I omitted from the table those appointments. There are two important departments of the Government that are not yet accounted for-Marine and Fisheries and Militia. The

1
only intervene in this debate, shall I say, at the invitation of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works. I am sure that in intervening I may well cast myself upon the sympathy of both sides of this House. I will tell my hon. friend why. He charged me with using strong language. That charge, coming from him at the present moment, is a very, very cutting charge. Why, Sir, I was literally afraid to listen to the quotations with which my hon. friend would back up his charge, because the point which has been raised by my right hon. leader has to do with a charge which, I think, some of us will characterize as mild. When we have to deal with a charge against a prominent public servant, that certain statements of his were unfair, untrue, dishonest and dishonourable, we are not dealing in lavender water in the way of language. The House will understand, therefore, that I really was afraid to hear my hon. friend quote what I had said. And what did this quotation amount to? It amounted to a statement made in this House on February 8 that the Liberal Bureau had not since the war broke out been issuing partisan literature.
Literature of any kind.

The nature of the assertion was as I have stated. Well, that they have been issuing literature between the outbreak of war in August and February 8, when I spoke, is proved by the hon. Minister of Public Works giving a quotation from a document issued on February 15. I appeal to my hon. friend; should he really blame me very much for not knowing on February 8 what was going to be printed on February 15? He charges me with dwelling in the shades of Cobden. In what wonderful shades does he live * or what' powers of prophecy does he possess that he enables his colleagues in this House to know on February 8 what is going to happen on February 15?

I Shall be glad to send
over to my hon. friend the issues of the Liberal Monthly for October, November and December.

If my hon. friend could
have found anything in the-issues of Novem-

ber and December to prove his case, he would have quoted it. Why did he quote from a copy of the Liberal Monthly published after I spoke? Because he could find nothing of a partisan nature in those published in November and December. But do my hon. friends read the Liberal Monthly, if their laughter means a contradiction of what I say? My hon. friend the Solicitor General says, Oh, yes. Then we may expect him to bring forth the partisan literature before even he, I am sure, will endeavour to prove a case against anything I said on February 8 by quoting something that was published on the 15th, a week afterwards. Hon. gentlemen opposite have an advantage over me, Mr. Speaker, in being regular students of the Liberal Monthly, for I do not happen to be a regular student of that publication. But before I made the statement in this House and after I made it I took occasion to speak to Mr. Godard, whose name has been mentioned in the course of this debate, and he assured me that nothing of a partisan nature had been printed. I myself read one or two issues published after the beginning of the war, and I found a very interesting historical account of the issues involved in the w.ar, dealt with in a manner similar to the way in which they were referred to in the very able speeches of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister and my hon. friend the Solicitor General. Was that partisan literature? I was using this matter regularly in patriotic meetings, as all of us were, not with a view to helping party, but with a view to the justification of the common cause of our country in the eyes of the world. That is what was issuing from the Liberal Bureau, so far as my information goes, and what has been issuing from it even up to the present moment. That applies to the period preceding February 8, and it was that period only that I referred to when I spoke on February 8.
I want to say a single word about a very narrow point which has been brought to the attention of this House, and I want tc say that word in a calm spirit. I do not admit the charge of my hon. friend that on the occasion to which he referred I used strong language, that is, judging language by such a criterion as I would bring to bear upon the language of my hon. friend. I do not admit using strong language, and I certainly do not want to use any on this occasion. I think that if the language used by the hon. minister with regard to Prof.
. Shortt had application anywhere, it was against those gentlemen who were using the figures on this side of the House, and not 41
against Prof. Shortt. I will tell my hon. friend why. I read Prof. Shortt's address as it was reported in the press of this city. My hon. friend should recognize that Prof. Shortt was dealing with the Civil Service, and quoted these figures not with a view to comparing the acts of this Government and those of the last Government, but with a view to showing, in an impartial and nonpartisan way, what he conceived to be the improper basis of the Civil Service. I am sure that hon. gentlemen opposite would not laugh at that if they had waited to hear what I had to say.
Professor Shortt in pointing out the unsatisfactory condition of the Civil Service in this country was following a very excellent example, he was following the example of the Prime Minister in many speeches made before 1911, speeches which in principle I am quite sure my right hon. friend would not now recede from. That is what I take in all fairness to be the object of Professor Shortt in delivering the address which he did on the Civil Service; and viewed from that standpoint the quotation of figures was an absolutely correct quotation of the figures as they had appeared in the returns up to that moment. He said there were
2.000	dismissals shown and there were 2,000 dismissals shown. Is that statement unfair, untrue, dishonest, or is the man making it dishonourable? He said there had been
10.000	new appointments and that is so.
Taking the place of resignations though.

If he had been wanting
to prove that they had been placed there not to fill the places of those who had resigned there would be some pertinence in what my hon. friend says now in interrupting; but Professor Shortt was simply dealing with the figures as he knew them, to show the unsatisfactory condition of the Civil Service. That is What I think to be the correct view of what Professor Shortt did. If the resignations, added to the dismissals, reduce the disparity between the persons leaving the service and the new appointments, it would weaken the argument which has been used by this side of the House about the extravagance of this Government. I concede that to my hon. friend. It would almost appear to me from the figures just given by the hon. member from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) that this is a matter which my hon. friend cannot afford to go into too deeply.
Oh, yes, we can.

It would also appear
to me-my hon. friend need not get excited, it is difficult for two of us to speak at once. I am saying that whether I have come from the shades of Cobden or elsewhere my hon. friend does not seem to know very much yet about this return or about what is going on in the Civil Service. However, I am not going into that. I simply wanted to make the admission I have made, that if the resignations added to the dismissals reduced the disparity between those receiving appointments and those going from the service that, would weaken an argument .used upon this side of the House; but, as far as a man claiming to be honourable, and I claim to be so, understands the meaning of language, that did not justify for one moment the language which was used by my hon. friend (Mr. Rogers); and if I have any knowledge of his character, the moment he sees that he will be the first man in Canada to withdraw the language. That is my opinion of him. It may be misplaced, but I hold it none the less. Nothing that Professor Shortt did justified the language which has been used by my hon. friend. I shall not go further into the question. I think I have cleared myself of the imputation, coming from a source that I was surprised to hear it come from on this particular occasion, of having used strong language. I made a simple statement, or I meant to convey to the House that from the bureau of the Liberal party at the time of the outbreak of war until the moment at which I was speaking, partisan literature had not been issued and that statement I repeat on the authority of those who have read the literature carefully. I am strongly disposed to believe this, because, as I have already pointed out, my hon. friend certainly did not quote any language in justification of his stating the opposite.
I shall not go into what my hon. friend called the progressive administration of this [DOT] Government. We may admit the adjective if he gives it a shade of meaning which I myself would be inclined to attach to it at the present moment. It has certainly been a progressive administration in the matter of appointments to the Civil Service by the most favourable construction upon the figures of that return that could be put upon them, the construction of my hon. friend himself. There has been no extra business done in Canada, and there has been no extra prosperity to justify-even this

gap of 4,000 employees between the time when the late Administration was in power and the present moment. A progressive administration? Well, we are going to speak on the Budget some of these days and we will have something to say about the progress of this Administration and the progress of Canada under it. As I said, I intervened for a specific purpose, and having accomplished it I shall express to my hon. friend the hope that when he introduces a comparatively harmless quotation from anything I have said in the future on an occasion when his own language, which I do not think he has justified, is of the strongest possible description, he will not charge me with having used strong language.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is very necessary, in order that there may be a fair and proper discussion on the question, that we should know what the language was which Professor Shortt, of the Civil Service Commission, used at the Peoples' Forum on the Sabbath evening, which has been brought to the consideration of this House this afternoon by the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). I have in my hand a copy of the Free Press of February 15, 1915. Professor Shortt's address was given on the evening of Sfinday, February 14. I read from the Free Press this report of Professor Shortt's remark:
I have met men in the Canadian Civil Service who, though they hold positions under the Government, were quite ready to admit that the Civil Service system was rotten.
He speaks of a Civil Service system which continued for a period of 15 years during all the time my right hon. friend was guiding the destinies of this country. He goes on to say:
Who took the place of the 2,000 civil servants who were retorted In the House the other day to have been dismissed from the service, and his reply to his own quesdon was just 10,000.
I ask hon. gentlemen to consider that language. He asked who took the places of 2,000 civil servants who, were dismissed, and he answered 10,000. In other words, Professor Shortt endeavoured to convey the meaning to the people of this country that
10,000	men were employed to do the work that had been done by those 2,000. His language had been evidently chosen with the greatest possible care in order to convey that impression, that under this Government, five men are employed doing the

*work that was done by one under the previous Administration. Could anything be more absolutely unfair-could anything be more absolutely-and I say it with consideration-untrue than that statement made by Professor Shortt? It is a statement which he must have known to be untrue. If he did not, then he had not read the return that had been laid before this House and which was the basis of the speech he was making at the Peoples' Forum; and if he made the statement without verifying it by reference to the return what can be said in his defence?
In view of the fact that the statement laid before the House in the return showed a very large number of dismissals, Professor Shortt, I say, was absolutely unjustified in making the assertions which he did make; and, further than that, his conduct in making that statement, I have no hesitation in saying to you, is unpardonable and indefensible, because he tried to create in the minds of the people of this country an impression of a state of facts, an impression that is absolutely false and untrue, because 10,000 men were not appointed, as he said in the careful language he used, to take the places of 2,000 men who had been dismissed.
When this statement was made public and the discussion of it commenced, I gave instructions to my deputy minister to have a careful statement made up with regard to my own department, showing the dismissals, the resignations, what . superannuations had taken place, how many deaths had occurred, how many new appointments had been made, and how those who had been appointed were accounted for. Let me read that statement, or give a synopsis of it to the House; and I might say to the hon. member for St. John that it is dated February 25, 1915.
I find that in the Department of Marine and Fisheries Marine Branch, including all Services and all departments, 464 have been dismissed from October 10, 1911, down to the present time. That number was entirely in the outside service; not a single dismissal from the inside service has taken place in my department since I became head of it in 1911.
Will that return be brought down?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It will be laid on the
table of the House at once. The dismissals in the Marine Branch of my 41J
department have been 464, a small number in comparison with the Liberal dismissals made in that department after hon, gentlemen opposite came into power in 1896. In passing, let me say that my hon. friend from Guysboro (Mr. Sinclair) regretted these resignations as being of a most improper character. No wonder my hon. friend is suspicious about resignations, for if he will look at the records of the Civil Service after the year 1896, he will find resignation after resignation that was forced at the very point of the bayonet. And not only that; but he will find that man' after man was removed from the fishery service on the ground that his services were no longer required, yet within a year his place was filled by some henchman of hon. gentlemen opposite. I have pointed out that there have been 464 dismissals in my Marine department. There have also been 340 resignations, and those resignations, so 'far as I know, are bona fide resignations; many of them made, no doubt, by men who had been taking a more active part in politics, and who, when the new Administration came into power, felt that, in view of the course they had taken, they were not justified in -taking office under this Government which they had abused so bitterly. These were all bona fide resignations. What else have we? We find that there were 289 vacancies caused by death, ill-health, old age, superannuation, etc., to which no allusion was made by Professor Shortt in his speech at the People's Forum. Since I came into office, there have been altogether 1,608 appointments in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. How are they accounted for? To fill the places of dismissed officers, 464 to fill vacancies by resignations, 340; to fill the vacancies caused by death, ill-health, old age, superannuation, etc., 289. That makes a total of 1,093 vacancies. The new appointments were 515. How were these new appointments accounted for? Why, my hon. friends opposite are responsible for more than half of the appointments, because they were in consequence of legislation and administrative acts of hon. gentlemen opposite. What are they? We required crews for the Estevan, Bellechasse, and Dollard, all of which were in course of construction and under contract when I became minister. The number of men in those crews is 102. Seven men have been appointed to the Cheticamp life-saving station, and four men to the Prince Rupert buoy depot staff. Twenty lighthouses have been completed, and twenty lightkeepers

appointed. Dredge No. 12 came into commission and required a crew of 31 men; Dredge No. 13, a crew of 31 men; the tug Lavaltrie, 16 men; the tug Laviolette, 16 men; Hopper barge No. 1, 14 men; making in all 241 new appointments made necessary in consequence,' of what took place before this Government came into power. Is there a single gentleman on the other side of the House who will take exception to the appointment of any of those men? Will any of them be so bold as to deny that the appointments are in the public interest, and necessitated by the progress and development of this country?
Let me read to my hon. friends opposite the list of wharves that have been transferred by the Public Works Department, Tinder the law, these wharves when built are transferred to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and we appoint wharfingers. Twenty-seven wharves have been transferred to our department, to which we have appointed 27 wharfingers. Was it not right that they should be appointed? Would it have been right to leave these wharves uncared for? And let me point out that the pay of these men has not cost the country one single extra dollar, because they are paid a percentage of the fees collected on the boats that use the wharf.
How c-ould Professor Shortt give these figures when the return had not been brought down?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
He had no right to make the statement he did without accurate information. Professor Shortt, an officer of this House, an official of this country, took occasion to make a speech that to my mind was animated principally by political animus, and which was for the purpose of discrediting the Government. Professor Shortt not only made a suggestion that was untrue, but practically made an untrue statement in not referring to the complete particulars. Let me continue my statement : fifteen harbours have been proclaimed during the same period, for which harbour masters were required to the number of 15. These men do not receive a salary from the Government, but a percentage of the fees collected at those harbours. To the meteorological stations throughout Canada, 51 new observers were appointed. The meteorological service has been extending very rapidly and is a most useful service. Will any one say that the small amount paid to these observers in the different parts of the country is unjustified, and not in the interests of Canada?

To the two new life-saving stations that have been established since this Government has been in power, 14 men were appointed, and let me say here that when my Estimates are before the House I never meet with any criticism for having too many stations in Canada; the criticism from hon. gentlemen opposite always is that the stations are too few. My hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) has appealed to me on several occasions for more of these stations on tne river and gulf of tne St. Lawrence.

The minister will admit
that it is most extraordinary that there should not be a Lie-saving station on-.the St. Lawrence. Only last year 1,200 lives were lost at Rimouski.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is exactly wnat 1
was saying. I am finding no fault with my hon. friend. I am saying that I am constantly appealed to by him, and other gentlemen who are anxious for life-saving stations in different parts of the country. My statement has been verified by the hon. member for Bonaventure. No one says that these stations should not have been established, and that the men should not have been appointed.
I find that at the various agencies throughout Canada 16 new clerks have been appointed in consequence of increasing business; and every year more buoys, more lights, and more aids to navigation are required. Parliament makes a very generous appropriation for that service, and we attempt to spend the money in the public interest. One new agent was appointed at Fort William. Fifty-eight new light stations have been established in Canada, to which 58 light keepers have been appointed. One deputy harbour master has been appointed, four port physicians, and four steamboat inspectors. We have a steamboat inspector up in the district north of Edmonton where there was none before, and where the owners of steamers had the greatest difficulty in getting certificates for their vessels. In addition to that, we have appointed two port wardens, who are paid by fees; three receivers of wrecks, who are also paid by fees; one inspecting engineer, and 20 additional clerks to the inside service at Ottawa, whose appointments were necessary in consequence of the increasing business of the department.
That is the statement as far as my own department is concerned. If this return had been on the table of the House-and I have no doubt that a similar statement could be made regarding other departments of the

Government-would Prof. Shortt have been justified in saying that there had been 464 officials dismissed and tKat to take their places 1,608 had been appointed? That would have been quite as fair play as to make the statement he did about 2,000 officials being dismissed and 10,000 appointed in their places. I have no doubt that any other department of the Government could make a statement quite as satisfactory as the statement I have made, and I challenge the most careful scrutiny of this statement which I shall lay on the table of the House. With the introduction of the free rural mail delivery system, with the introduction of the parcel post system, with the extension to the people in outside parts of the facilities and advantages of the post office service, and with the enormous increase that has taken place in the customs revenue, would we not have expected Prof. Shortt, if he had wanted to be fair, to have said to those that he was addressing at the People's Forum on that Sabbath evening:	Of course, as the
country grows, extra officials must be appointed, and with a revenue to be collected $40,000,000 greater than it was before, or with a post office service whose work and income are largely increasing, it is only natural to expect that the country must employ officials to carry on the larger business the several departments have to do. No such idea apparently occurred to the learned professor. He was anxious to make the statement, and after carefully studying it beforehand, and after evidently reading the return which was put before the House, he stated that 2,000 men had been dismissed and that five men had been appointed to take the place of every man who had been dismissed, without reference to the increase in the growth of the business of the country, without reference to the resignations that had taken place, without reference to the superannuations that had taken place, the deaths that had taken place, and other causes <as a result of which officials had to retire from the department in which they had been employed.
This discussion has been precipitated by the right hon. leader of the Opposition. He has brought Prof. Shortt in question before this House. He has brought the whole matter up for consideration. After my experience as a minister of the Crown for a period extending over three years I have no hesitation in saying that I do not think- and I think this is the opinion of my department, when I say my department, I
mean the permanent men in the department -that Prof. Shortt possesses those qualities that make him an efficient member of the Civil Service Commission. In my department we have lived up to the Civil Service Act. When vacancies have occurred we have asked for a recommendation from the Civil Service Commission, and in more than one instance where we have asked that men be sent to the department men have been sent by the Civil Service Commission who were entirely unfit for the work for which we wanted them and to which they were assigned by Prof. Shortt.
Probably Prof. Shortt might have discharged the duties of his position with more credit to himself and more satisfaction to those who are the permanent heads of the different departments had he paid that attention to his duties which the importance of his position demanded. Let me read to this House a letter which, on the 22nd August last, and after the strongest representations had been made to me by the permanent head of my department, I addressed to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister:
Dear Sir Robert:
On the 20th of this month a letter was addressed by the Deputy Minister of Naval Affairs to the secretary of the Civil Service Commission respecting the issue of a certificate of qualification in favour of Mr. Charles Savary whom it is proposed to promote from subdivision A of the second division to subdivision B of the first division.
Mr. Savary is in command of the Cartier, and is in Ottawa at the present time and prepared to undergo his examination.
In reply to the request made by the Deputy Minister a letter was received from the secretary of the Civil Service Commission stating that it would be duly submitted to the commissioners on their return from abroad. Both of the commissioners are absent from Ottawa at the present time and we are informed that nothing in the way of promotion would be done until they returned. It seems to me most undesirable that the work of the commission should be suspended, and arrangements should ha made that one of the commissioners at least he in the office at all times. The action of the commissioners is causing us considerable inconvenience, and no doubt other branches of the Civil Service are being also inconvenienced.
I thought it proper to call your attention to this matter so that on the return of the chairman of the commission arrangements might be made to the effect that that office should always be open and the work carried on.
It may he stated that absolutely nothing is being done through the Civil Service Commission at the present time beyond the merest routine. It seems to me a little less than disgraceful that a time like this should be selected by the commissioners to leave Ottawa when most of the departments of the Government are exerting themselves to the utmost, and that at

such a critical time the important duties of the Civil Service should be neglected.
At the time to which the hon. minister alludes, was not Prof. Shortt absent in the old country on Government business?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
On his own business, not on Government business, I am informed. I took it to be my duty, in view of the inconvenience caused in our department, as represented to me by the permanent head of the department, to call the attention of the Prime Minister to the state of affairs on August 22 last, long before Prof. Shortt had delivered his speech at the People's Forum or put himself in a position of antagonism and hostility to the Government. That is what I have said regarding his qualifications for the position, and I have no hesitation in repeating that statement in the most explicit terms as the result of the experience that I have had in dealing with the Commission.
Now, Mr. Speaker, would it not have been fair for the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), when reading to this House the figures he had made up regarding the employees of the Department of the Interior, to have read the note there is on the statement that has been laid on the table of the House in regard to the Department of the Interior? The statement, after giving the number of men dismissed and the appointments and so on, said:
Appointments Include several hundred temporary employees at Ottawa who do not appear among the "dismissed" or "resigned." They were employed under the Civil Service Act for six months or so and allowed to go when their time expired.	*
It would not have served the purpose of the hon. - gentleman to have read to the House that note of explanation in the report handed in by the Minister of the Interior. Nor would it have served his purpose, I suppose, to have read in the return of the Civil Service Commissioners a statement showing that when one man resigned eight were appointed to take his place. Possibly there was work for all those men to do; but any one could make the argument against Prof. Shortt in his own department that for one official who resigned eight officials were appointed to take his place, because the statement appears in the report that one resigned and eight extra employees were appointed to positions in that department. I do not suppose those eight men were appointed to take the place of the one man who

was dismissed. I presume that the work of the Civil Service Commissioners has been increased as the work of the other departments of this Government has been increased, and that therefore they have found it necessary to appoint extra oflicials for the purpose of properly carrying on the work of their department. I do not want to trespass further upon the time of the House. I have given to the House the statement of the Marine Branch of my own department. I regret that it was not laid on the table of the House before; but possibly it is well that such has not been the case, because it would not have been up to date, and I understand that my hon. friend the member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley) raised some point because he claimed that the figures of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) were not up to date.
Speaking from the standpoint of my own department, and I believe I can speak for all the members of this Government, I say that we are prepared for the most careful investigation of this matter, especially as to the new appointments that have been made. They were made in the public interest, and were necessitated by the growth and development of the public work of this country.

I listened as attentively as I could to the figures given by my hon. friend as to the appointments in his own department, and as I made them out, after he had shown us the necessity for the appointment of various people, there was still left about 100 entirely unaccounted for.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: It is a position for which friends may make a recommendation.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
These stations are scattered all over Canada, and no observer has been appointed except on the recommendation of Mr. Stupart, director of the Meterological Service.
Two life-saving stations, 14 men ; additional clerks required at the various agencies, 15 men. New agent at Fort William.
Is that a new agent?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. We used to pay a sum of money indirectly to some other official. In view of the importance of the harbour, we desired to appoint an agent of our own.
Light stations, new, 58; deputy harbour master, 1; port physicians, 4; steamboat inspectors, 4; port wardens . (paid by fee), 2; receiver of wrecks (paid by fees), 3; signal service operators, 2; inspecting engineer, 1; additions, inside service, 20; additions, outside service, 8.
The Canadian Government steamer Arranmore, the steamer that we purchased on account of the extra work that had to be done in Hudson strait and Hudson bay, required a crew of 47 men.

-You did not mention that in your first statement.
Mr, HAZEN: I intended to do so. That ought to make a total of 274 new appointments.

It seems to me that my hon. friends the Minister of 5 p.m. Public Works and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries have both departed somewhat from the point brought up by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. The object which I understand my right hon. friend had in view and which he sought to accomplish was that, in fairness to the gentleman occupying such an important position in this country as the chairman of the Civil Service Commission, a gentleman who, while appointed by the Governor in Council, yet is not subject to the control of the Government, but to the control of the two Houses of Parliament, ought to be given an opportunity of justifying the language
which he used upon the occasion referred to.
That, I understand, was the point of the suggestion made by my right hon. friend.
It must be borne in mind that Professor Shortt is not a member of this House. It must be borne in mind that he has been attacked behind his back, attacked where he has no opportunity to defend himself by justifying his statements or proving the truth of the statements he is alleged to have made, and which I have no doubt he did make, at the Forum upon the occasion to which hon. gentlemen have referred.
Were the members of the Government present at the Forum when Professor Shortt attacked their policy?

That was an assembly
which was open to the whole public, including any member of the Government.

The meetings of this
House are open to the public, including Professor Shortt.

But if he spoke in the gallery he would be arrested. Professor Shortt has the right, as any man has, upon the invitation of this House, to appear at the bar to explain his conduct. It does seem to me that the suggestion of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition is only fahAthat this House, together with the Senate, having control over Professor Shortt so far as his continuance in office is concerned, not only has a right to appoint a committee to allow Professor Shortt to be heard and to take the evidence which may be given, but it is its duty to do so. It would be entirely out of place for Professor Shortt to make any reply to the statements made to-day by the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. It would be unseemly for him to do so. When he was interviewed by the [DOT] newspaper reporter after what had taken place in this House during my observations on the Budget, he very properly said he would not enter into a discussion on the subject, that the statement which he had made was a statement simply based upon the returns which had been laid before the House.

The hon. gentleman has hardly completed Professor Shortt's statement, as given in the interview. According to the interview which he gave out to the Free Press, he went further. He not only said he was simply quoting from the return, but said also:

I had no information other than was contained in the return-for instance, I had no information about resignations.
If he had the return, he had the information about resignations.
He may or may not so far as my knowledge would enable me to speak, because unfortunately we have not been able to see the return.
Professor Shortt did.
Not the return of all the departments-that has not been brought down.
Then, why did he make the statement ?
He made it from the returns which he had seen, returns brought down by the departments to which he had access.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That return showed 3,500 resignations.
Oh, oh.

A pall of despair had settled over the country and people were leaving by hundreds, by thousands and by tens of thousands. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works was there at that time; he knows that what I am saying is true. I speak as one who knows, because I was one of the pioneers in that country.
I went there as far back as 1881, and I have kept in close touch with it ever since. Sir, it was not until a vigorous, progressive and broad immigration policy was inaugurated by the Liberal party that the western country began to develop and its population began to increase. Immigrants came in from the United States, from England, and from practically all civilized countries, and a rapid and continuous expansion took place. That prosperity, progress and development continued until not many months after the present Government came into power; but to-day, in our great western country, and in the east as well, the conditions are practically the same as they were in 1895, not long before the Liberal party came into power.
Was the hon. gentleman supporting the late Government in 1895?
Many people, Sir, supported the late Government in sorrow, because they saw-
Oh, oh.
-because they saw that the late Government was doing nothing for the development and expansion of the country.
Hear, hear.
That was in 1895; that would be about the time that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister,was supporting the Liberal party.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: And my hon. friend himself was supporting the Conservative party at the same time. A fair exchange, perhaps.

I will not go into that sorrowful tale, with which my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is so familiar; besides, we have heard so much about it that it is hardly worth while. That was nineteen odd years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: But my hon. friend was reproaching the Prime Minister.

I did not do so until the Minister of Labour called my attention to the matter, and when one becomes

reminiscent it is not at all out of the way
for him to consider the position occupied by other persons at the time referred to. That is my only excuse for referring to a subject of no importance "so far as this question is concerned. But the point I want to make is that under the Liberal administration, during the whole 15 years of development, prosperity, increased population, increased business, increased customs revenue, increased postal revenue, increased inland revenue, increased revenue in all departments, there never was anything like the increase in the number of employees in a corresponding period of time that there has been during the three years that this Government has been in office.
My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has given a list of appointments that have been made in his department. He says that they were to take the places of persons who had been dismissed or who had resigned, or to carry on new branches of the department. But my hon. friend forgets that in addition to that there were a number of employees who were in ill health and a number who had grown old in the service and were incapable of discharging their duties any longer. The services of many of these men, who, as we know, are allowed to remain in the service, doing comparatively little work, might very well be dispensed with. Was it necessary, therefore, for my hon. friend to appoint strong, vigorous young men and women in the place of the 289 old persons who apparently had become unfit for further service? He not only makes these additional appointments of 515 persons, but presumably he fills the places of 289 employees who have grown too old to be of service in the department by appointing younger persons. One would think, therefore, that he must have had a large number of employees in his department whose services were not absolutely necessary. It is common knowledge in this country that this Government has been earnestly endeavouring to make jobs for scores and hundreds of people in various sections of Canada,
No.

I venture to say that the hon. gentleman who protests himself knows as well as I do that this is a fact, and I have no doubt that the same condition prevails in his constituency. Demands were made upon these gentlemen; improperly they yielded to them, and the result has been this enormous and unnecessary
[Mr. Pusjsley.l
increase in the number of employees in the various departments. What does that mean? You have 11,000 [DOT] more employees in the various departments of the Government than there were when this Government came into office in 1911. What does it mean? Is it too much to say that outside of those who are paid by fees, their salaries would average at least $800 or perhaps $1,000 each, taking the whole 11,000? At $1,000 each then, it means the enormous sum of $11,000,000 which has been added to the ordinary current expenditure of this country. It does seem to me that the burthen resting on hon. gentlemen opposite is not simply to condemn us because we bring these matters up, but to show us what have been the increases in the different departments and to justify those increases. To-day the Prime Minister made the motion that you leave the Chair in order to precipitate this discussion. He might, had he desired, have allowed the limited discussion to go on as to what should be done so far 'as Professor Shortt was concerned; but when my right hon. friend moved, that you leave the Chair, immediately the Minister of Public Works entered upon a general discussion as to whether these appointments were justifiable or not, aijd spoke of the increase of the business in his department. He has been followed by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. But they still leave us without this report; they cannot even tell us where it is. It is their business to keep control of it, and, if they cannot get the report, to furnish a copy of it. I have no doubt there is in the Department of Secretary of State a copy of this report. The Secretary of State never submits a return to this House without keeping a copy. I have no doubt there is in each department a copy of the report sent to the Department of State in order that they might make up the general report covering all departments. Is it unreasonable to ask that we should be furnshed with a copy of that report? Is it unreasonable to ask that this House should have an opportunity of looking into that report? It seems to me most unreasonable that we should be denied that opportunity. It looks as if hon. gentlemen were simply seeking to cast dust into the eyes of the people of this country in making assertions of a general character without giving us an opportunity of going into details and questioning the correctness of the statements which they make. I and other members of the House would like an opportunity to see the returns from the different depart-

ments. There is no excuse for not bringing down those returns before this late date. The returns were moved for by a member of this House at the session of 1913-14, but up To to-day, up to this very moment, we have not got the return of the Departfnent of Marine and Fisheries; although my hon. friend the minister has addressed the House with regard to the subject, we find that we have not even his return before us, and we only got the return from the department of the Postmaster General to-day. There are some other departments the returns for which are not yet before the House. There is no justification for that delay. What is the use of members having the right to move for returns when they are to be delayed month after month, the delay running over into the following year. That is the case with returns which were moved for in 191314, so far as this subject is concerned. It is not fair to this House, or to those who wish to discuss the matter, that this return should not be here. Notwithstanding that the returns are not here, knowing as I do something with regard to the condition of this country, I submit that there is no excuse for the enormous number of appointments which have been made. Even in the case of the Department of Public Works, I submit there is no excuse for such a large increase in the number of appointments. The Minister of Public Works speaks of the increase in the work of dredging, and he refers to an increase of from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000. My hon. friend must be wrong in that, because if he will take the Estimates, which can be found in the Blue Book which has been submitted to Parliament, he will find that under dredging, on page 72, there is only $2,307,000. Would my hon. friend be good enough to state how he makes up the difference? Maybe he is right, and it is not contained on page 72, but in some other portion of the Blue Book.
The report which I sent over to my hon. friend was made up by the deputy minister, Mr. Hunter. I looked it over with him, and I am satisfied it is correct in every detail.

At page 72 it gives the dredging for the maritime provinces, for Ontario and Quebec, for Manitoba arid Saskatchewan and Alberta and for British Columbia; it gives the cost of dredging plant in the maritime provinces and the other provinces, and the total is $2,307,000. It may be that- under capital account, on harbours and rivers, there is some additional dredging which may give the increased
amount, but it is certainly not under the head of dredging. My hon. friend says a large increase in the staff has been necessary for the purpose of rushing along the public buildings. I submit that is not justified by the interests of the country. When I was minister there was a large staff in the architectural branch. While the officials worked pretty zealously, I never saw any urgent necessity for making increases in the staff, and I do not think it was necessary for the minister to make increases in that branch of the department.

There was occasion for increase by reason of the fact that during the term that you were Minister of Public Works a large number of plans were made by outside architects. We have tried to . change that and to have the plans made inside the department, as far as possible. Therefore the department required an increase in the staff for carrying out the work, especially in view of the fact that the department as a whole was spending only $14,000,000 in 1911, while in 1914 it was spending $23,000,000-just double the amount.

My hon. friend is spending double the amount of money. That raises another question which we have already discussed as to whether that enormous expenditure of $28,000,000 is really necessary in the interests of the country. It all shows that when this Government came into power they were crazed by the degree of prosperity which they found all around them. They were like a young man, somewhat improvident, coming into a great inheritance; and they went to work to spend money just as rapidly as they could, and so they discovered at once that the late Minister of Public Works had not a sufficiently large staff, he had not enough architects to spend all this Government wanted to spend. The Department of Railways and Canals had not enough engineers to carry out their large ideas in connection with development, so far as that department was concerned, and they proceeded at once, not only to ask Parliament to vote this large additional sum of money, but to enlarge the staff of architects and engineers.
They proceeded right here in the city of Ottawa to rent a large number of new buildings, although when in Opposition they criticised the late Government for the number of buildings which we had rented. They told us then that we had more accommodation than was necessary for properly carrying on the work of the country, but when these gentlemen came into power they at

once proceeded to rent more buildings at a larger rental than we paid. These buildings necessitate a large number of elevator men, a large number of furnace men, and a large number of caretakers, and add enormously, and I think unnecessarily, to the expenses of the country. What my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works ought to have done was to have gone along slowly with the officials already in the employ of the Government. He ou^ht to have been content to spend $12,000,000 in his department. That is a large sum of money. The minister tells us that the Government has erected eighty public buildings in Canada during the past year. Let the minister tell us how many of those buildings were urgently required to meet the public service, and how many of the postal building that have-been erected throughout Canada were actually required. A great many of these post office buildings have been erected in towns whore accommodation was formerly rented for a moderate amount, and served the public interest very well. I have in mind the case of a public building which the Minister of Public Works has erected in a county where accommodation was formerly rented. I do not think the rental could have exceeded $100, and yet the Minister of Public Works has erected a public building there at a cost of some $35,000 or $40,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In what county?

In my old county of
Kings, N.B. The building is in a small village containing but a few hundred people. A beautiful village it is true, but when I was Minister of Public Works I had stated to Parliament that I proposed putting up there a pretty one-story building to cost about $5,000, which I thought would be ample for the purpose.
Did you ever build one for $5,000?
That was the first occasion on which I thought of putting up a building in such a small town as that.
What about Humboldt?

Humboldt is two,
three, four, five times the size of the place at which this building had been erected at a cost of some $35,000 or $40,000. What does this mean? Besides the cost of the building there is the cost of heating, the cost of a caretaker, and repairs have to be made from time to time. It will probably mean an expense ten times greater than
fMr. Pugs'ey.]
was previously incurred in that place. And that is merely an instance of what has been done all over this country since this Government came into power. They have erected buildings in places which they stated, when in Opposition, did not require public buildings, and so have added to the public expense all around.
Before taking my seat I wish to say a word or to further on behalf of Professor Shortt, and in support of the suggestion which my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition has made. I for one do not believe that Professor Shortt cares one iota for this Government or for this Opposition. When we were in office, I never saw any evidence that Professor Shortt showed any favouritism towards the late Government. In fact, in many cases the recommendations 1 made were turned down by the Civil Service Commission. But I recognized that the Civil Service Commission was an independent body entitled to the exercise of its own judgment. I recognized 'that it was when it was proposed to make the Civil Service Commission an independent body, that both sides of this House supported the proposition and expected the Civil Service Commission to take .the Civil Service as far as possible out of politics.
