I have never seen any evidence of partiality towards the Liberal party from that Commission, and I do not believe that Professor Shortt's remarks on the occasion referred to were influenced in the slightest degree by his feeling in favour of the Liberal party or against the Conservative party. I do not think such an idea ever entered his head for a single moment.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has referred to the necessity of having some member of the Commission here continually to attend to business. I notice that in the Statutes of 1912 it was provided that the old Civil Service Act should be amended by giving the Governor General power to appoint three members to the Civil Service Commission instead of two. May I ask if that appointment has ever been made?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, it has not.

Why not? My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries; has read a letter complaining that some of the commissioners were absent. Why has the Government not exercised its power and appointed an additional member of the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will give my hon. friend some information when he gets through.

I shall have no trouble in getting through before six o'clock. I would ask that complete returns from all departments he brought down; not these fragmentary returns, a return from one department one week and another return from another department the next week. If the Government will comply with the order that was passed by this House upwards of a year ago and bring down complete returns so that we can examine them, and if the Government will appoint a day for the discussion of the necessity of making this vast number of appointments, I think they will find a readiness on this side of the House to meet them in that discussion, and to take up the oases of individuals in the different provinces. But I think we have a right to say that we should have these returns before us, so that we can speak with intelligence and a degree of certainty in the matter. I thank my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) for having, after a good deal of effort, dug out some information from an unwilling Government. We have this fact: some 21,000 appointments have been made to fill the vacancies caused by some 10,000 dismissals, deaths, desertions and resignations. That is something, at all events, upon which we can go and something in regard to which I think we have a very good foundation for appealing to the people of this country. I think it justifies the charge which has already been made during this debate that this Government in its appointments at all events, if not in its carrying on of the general administration of affairs, has been guilty of reckless disregard in the way the people's money has been expended. Through mismanagement, and through failure to have due regard to those principles of economy which ought to govern those having charge of the administration of affairs, the Government have brought this country into a position which should give very grave concern to the people, and lead us even now to consider whether it would not be possible to engage on a work of retrenchment, by means of -which many millions of dollars might be annually saved to the people of this country.

Mr. Speaker, it is no more than justice to the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) to say that the example of debating which he has given the House in the last half-hour is not at all up to the standard of which he is capable upon a subject that he is really interested in and upon which he has something to say. The
hon. gentleman was under the unpleasant necessity of switching from the point of the discussion, into which the Opposition now wish they had never plunged, to a subject as dull, monotonous and time-worn as he could discover, and then engaging in a pathetic effort to drag that discussion along its weary length to as near six o'clock as possible. The discussion arose, with the interposition of the right hon. the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) on behalf of the chairman of the Civil Service Commission who has been attacked in this House because, on the basis of a return- and one return alone-he made a public statement, though a civil servant of this country, that was at variance with the facts as shown in that return. If he made a statement at variance with the facts, plainly at variance with the facts and calculated to deceive and made it knowingly he made a statement which was dishonourable, dishonest and untrue. Did he make a statement at variance with the facts? Was it plainly at variance with the facts, and must he not have known that it was at variance with the facts? That is the point before the House, nothing more and nothing less. The statement he made, quoted in two newspapers in the city of Ottawa, was that the return, which toe treated as one entity and no more, a copy of which return I hold in my hands, showed that the Government of Canada, since it came into office, had dismissed 2,000 employees of the Civil Service and in then places had put 10,000. That is the report of the Citizen; that is the report of the Ottawa Free Press. That statement is false, that statement is untrue, that statement is misleading, and that statement, on the professor's own showing, was false to tois own knowledge. He says that he had the return, that he knew what was in the return, that that was all he knew, and taking that return and knowing what was in it, he said that there were 2,000 dismissals replaced with 10,000 appointments and nothing said about resignations. Both sentences were false, and he must have known that they were false because he had the return, and what some other return may say has nothing to do with that paper. What does the hon. member (Mr. Pugsley) expect to do for Professor Shortt by asking for an additional return which he says will show that what Professor Shortt said about this return is true? How can an additional return vary the facts of the present return? False! Two thousand dismissals were made, almost 4,000 resignations took

place which we*re mentioned, but beyond the dismissals and beyond the resignations there was an intervening hiatus which Professor Shortt owed it to himself and his audience to explain-the number of deaths, the number of superannuations and more than all, the number of temporary appointments-men who go on for certain purposes temporarily and then are left off the serivce. Why, take, the report of the Post Office Department alone. Who is there who does not know, and no one better than Professor Shortt, that in every town and city in Canada at Christmas time there are many appointments made to the Post Office service? In my own city of about 7,000 people there are every year added to the post office staff one or two. Take that proportion all over Canada and thousands would intervene between resignations and appointments and the total number of-appointees is thereby accounted for.
Does my hon. friend mean to say that these temporary clerks appointed at Christmas time in towns and cities are included under the heading of appointments?

I certainly mean to
say so and I mean to say further that Professor Shortt knew they were so included.
They are not so included.
I have the Postmaster General's authority for the statement that they are so included, and I prefer to rely upon it.
Is my hon. friend referring to the report brought down by the Postmaster General to-day?

No, I am referring to this return. The hon. gentleman will see, if he looks at the return, that in many instances it is pointed out that temporary appointments are included and that the employees are of the class to which I have referred.
The post office return is not in the one that my hon. friend has.
Very well.

Was the post
office return in the statement to which Professor Shortt referred?

The post office return
was brought down to-day.

Mr. 'CLARK: Then, how could Professor Shortt .know that these temporary appointments were included in the return?

Because it says so in
several of the departments included in the return itself. Now I will read to my hon. friend from Red Deer. I intend to read to him a lot more just a little later, but I will read to him from the return of the Department of the Interior:
Dismissals, 309 ; resignations, 374 ; d&serters, none; punished, none; appointments, 1,651.
There would be a difference of 800 or 900 men. Then, it is said:
The appointments include several hundred temporary employees at Ottawa who do not appear among the " dismissed " or " resigned " They were employed under the Civil Service Act for six months or so and allowed to go wheh their term expired.
In a number of other returns the relation of similar facts will be found and Professor Shortt owed it to his audience and to this Government to make that statement and not the statement he did make.
That does not refer to the postal clerks who were appointed at Christmas time and to whom my hon. friend referred.

My statement as to
postal clerks is absolutely correct. In the return in which postal clerks are referred to the postal clerks taken on at Christmas are included.

But not in the return to
which Professor Shortt referred.
No, but the same principle applies in both cases and that is what Professor Shortt ignored or rather suppressed. Now is my hon. friend satisfied?
I am satisfied that my hon. friend was wrong.

It takes very little to
satisfy the hon. member. I interposed in this discussion-

Will my hon. friend
allow me to ask him a question?
Certainly. I make a very great effort to extend to my hon. friend the courtesy which he extended to me.

I thank my hon. friend for his forgiving Spirit. He said he wanted to have a conversation with my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean). My hon. friend says he has a copy of a return which none of us on this

side of the House are able to find. Will he he good enough to have a copy of his copy made and laid on the table so that it may be accessible?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I went to get a copy of the return myself a few days ago and I found it was in the possession of the leader of the Opposition.

I will say to
my right hon. friend that he found nothing of the kind. I had a partial return, hut the main return I never had.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I was informed that it had been in the possession of my right hon. friend and that he had had copies made of it. I asked that one of the copies which had been prepared should be furnished to me and it was furnished to me.
My right hon. friend was more clever than I was, because I never had such a report.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My right hon.
friend was not so diligent about the matter as- I was.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
-'The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, when this matter was first broached it did not seem one of very great importance, but as the discussion developed, and as two ministers of the Crown, speaking with great deliberation, and without doubt, realizing the weight their words will carry throughout the Dominion, have made certain charges against the chairman of the Civil Service Commission, it seems to me incumbent on this House to seriously consider the matter. If I understood correctly the position of the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), the members of the Civil Service Commission are beyond the control of the Government and can be discharged only on the joint address of the House of Commons and the Senate. It is not my intention to discuss the evidence submitted or the statements made here this afternoon; but I should not be discharging my duty as I see it if I did not explain to the House through you, Sir, that my spirit revolts at the finding of a man guilty on the ex-parte statement of a newspaper correspondent. If the chairman of the. Civil Service Commission is guilty of the improprieties alleged; if Professor Shortt has drawn to himself since he came to Ottawa
the attributes that he is alleged to bear, then I think it is the duty of this House to take into consideration the place that he ought to occupy. Those of us who were more or less interested in Civil Service reform welcomed the appointment of a Civil Service Commission. But when the chairman of the Civil Service Commission is charged with having so far forgotten himself as to become biased and partisan, it seems to me not unreasonable that an inquiry should be set on foot. If the ministers were sincere in the allegations that they have placed before the House and the country this afternoon, then it is incumbent upon the Prime Minister to name a committee of this House, if necessary, to act in conjunction with a committee of the Senate, to inquire fully ipto the conduct of the chairman of the Civil Service Commission. He owes it not only to this House and to each one of us who must bear a certain responsibility for the discharge of the duty of the Civil Service Commission, but he owes it to the country as well. For, if the Civil Service Commission breaks down it must be more difficult for the right hon. leader of the Government to put into effect one of the planks of his Halifax platform -Civil Service reform. I wish to say to the House and to the country through you, that if the condition is as serious as was represented to us this afternoon, I believe that it is incumbent upon the Ministry to name a committee of this kind or to call Professor Shortt before the Bar of this House so that there may be an opportunity for an investigation. If the charges made in this House this afternoon are proven to be true, no one will be more willing than I to see Professor Shortt removed from office. But if the charges are not true, it is not necessary for me to advise the House what should be done, because hon. gentlemen at all times know the courtesy that is demanded towards men who have been wrongly assailed.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance) :

speechtext:

turn, and I am sure that a memorandum from him will be entirely satisfactory to all the members of this House. And I desire, in fairness to myself as I have said, and in fairness to my department, to place the memorandum on Hansard. It is as follows:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Additional buildings, as
follows: Central station, Blackburn building, 500 Sussex street building, Eideau club, 69 Vittoria street, Eobinson building, old Union Bank building, 241 Wellington street, Hope building, 6th flat, 223 Queen street building, 328 Queen street building, Quebec Bank building, 265J Wellington street, Masonic Temple building, Booth building, 14 Kent street building, 105 Vittoria street building, Journal building,. 27 Cliff street building, old museum building, biological laboratory, McKay street building, two extra flats in Imperial building, new wing, East block. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I dismissed none of them. Since I took office I have refrained from

even considering such a trifling question as the dismissal of a charwoman for partisan or other reasons. My hon. friend's suggestion rather shows what would be in his mind if he were here and I were there.
I think my hon. friend said that seven were dismissed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They were dismissed for
cause by the officers of the department.
For political partisanship?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, not for political partisanship. The hon. member for the city of St. John rather seemed to suggest that the renting of the buildings may have been unnecessary. The trouble with the hon. member for St. John and certain other gentlemen on the opposite side of the House, who have spoken not only on this occasion but recently in [DOT] connection with the Budget debate as well, is that they evidently labour under the delusion that when they stopped governing, this country stopped growing. I would point out to my hon. friends that the sun continues its daily journey east and west through the heavens, even though a clock may have run down. The hon. member for Red Deer threatens to meet us at Philippi in the Budget debate. We will be there. Let me point out to him that the year before this Government took office the total trade of this country was $750,000,000. The year we took office it was $850,000,000; the next year it was $1,000,000,000, and the next year $1,100,000,000. When we took office the revenue of Canada was $135,000,000; the second year it was $168,000,000-the best by far in the history of the Dominion-and the next year it was $163,000,000. This year, of course, we have the war.
Oh, oh; the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am surprised to learn
that hon. gentlemen opposite do not seem to be aware that a war is now proceeding. It has been borne in on me on many occasions; it was borne in on me yesterday. Intellectual as my hon. friend the member for St. John is, he lacks the vision and imagination. While the great allied fleet has been smashing its way through the Dardanelles on the way to Constantinople, and, according to the despatches, the Allies and Turkish troops are in conflict on the plains of Troy, where gods and heroes contended in prehistoric times, what was my hon. friend discussing in this House? The duty upon squid. Reductio ad absurdum- 42
fertilizers and squid. Having regard to the fact that there is in progress a war not only greater than any that has ever occurred in the history of the world, but greater than the aggregate of all wars that have ever taken place I would point out that the people will expect hon. gentlemen to get a proper sense of the perspective of the situation.
That is not fair.
What were you doing?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would suggest that they get a proper sense of perspective in regard to the great war in which we are now engaged. But, to come back to the subject of our discussion, which is* at least more important than the matter of squid-
I think the Budget mentioned squid.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It does, but my hon. friend did not understand the Budget.
The people will.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, they do understand it. I would suggest to my hon. friends that they go to the reading room, turn over the pages of the newspapers issued in various parts of the Dominion, and see how many editorials they will find on the Budget.
Quite a number.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not many. Some may be found in the paper of my hon. friend in Montreal, but not in many other papers. I wish to say this with regard to the matter under consideration.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friends desire that I should speak to the question, I must ask them not to interrupt; if they interrupt, I purpose answering them. I am like the Scotchman who said he was a peaceful man, but if there was any fighting to do he was not going to take any blows lying down.
With regard to the matter under immediate consideration, I desire to say this: I have known Professor Shortt for many years. I have never on any occasion spoken ill of him; I have always spoken well of him. My right hon. friend called attention to a very important matter this afternoon in introducing this subject. He said that Professor Shortt was amenable not to this Government but to Parliament. As I understand the situation, the assertion of my right hon. friend is correct. I desire

65S

to say further that I have no intention whatever of prejudging this matter. I have seen no contradiction by Professor Shortt of the report of his speech. On the contrary, I have before me an article published in the Ottawa Free Press of February 26 purporting to be an interview with Professor Shortt. There is no denial, so far as I can ascertain, of the report which was published in th.e Citizen on Monday, February 15, the day after Professor Shortt's remarks were made. If Professor Shortt is, as I believe he is, responsible to Parliament, that does not necessarily mean that his actions or conduct may not be criticised in a proper ease by this House. But I would say that, occupying, as he does, a position quasijudicial in its character, it is absolutely incumbent upon Prof. Shortt, or any man who may occupy that position, that he should not in any way- intermeddle, or give the appearance of intermeddling, in party politics, that he should avoid the appearance of being influenced in the slightest degree by partisan considerations, in any statement that he may make. Without going into the question of whether he intentionally made these statements or not, Prof. Shortt is a man of very high intelligence, and he might have known, in fact I think he should have known, that in speaking as he did, he was placing before the public a statement which those to whom it might be of political advantage to use would not hesitate to avail themselves of, as they did, Mr. Speaker, as shown by the Minister of Public Works this afternoon.
Now, of what was Prof. Shortt talking? According to this report he was talking of patronage. Taking my own department, because I have risen only for the purpose of defending it, any one might infer, in so far as the returns from my department form a part of the total returns brought down, that, in the exercise of political patronage, I had dismissed twelve or more employees in the Finance Department and had replaced them with something over two hundred. Now, that would be what the public would gather from the statements made by Prof. Shortt, or alleged to have been made by him, and, so far as I can ascertain, not contradicted by him, in this report which has formed the subject of discussion this afternoon. As I have said, a man in Prof. Shortt's position should be absolutely judicial, absolutely impartial; he should have made his statement in such a way that if the naked figures went out they would be accompanied by such

explanation as	would	set	all thefacts clearly	before	the public.
He failed to do so and the impression went out to the country that this Government had dismissed 2,000 employees and substituted in their place 10,000 employees, and the public would naturally draw the conclusion, and hon. gentlemen opposite fostered that view, because they availed themselves at once of the information, that we had deliberately dismissed, under our powers of patronage, 2,000 employees and substituted 10,000 without additional duties. I say, and I go no further than this because I am not sufficiently familiar with all the facts and hesitate to prejudge the case, that Professor Shortt, in my judgment, was guilty at least of indiscretion, in making a statement of this kind without making also the necessary explanations, which have been given by my colleagues and myself here this afternoon? It is absolutely unfair to us, and has been made use of, presumably to our political disadvantage, by hon. gentlemen opposite, who now make on a question of privilege, an attack upon the Minister of Public Works for resenting the statement which has been used, as 1 have said, presumbaly to the disadvantage of the Government. My own view is that a man occupying a judicial or quasi-judicial position in this country should not interfere in politics at all, and should avoid statements that will reflect upon either the Government of the day or the Opposition. I would ask that from judges on the Bench, and I think we can ask no less from members of the Civil Service Commission.
The hon. member for Bed Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) was disposed to take a charitable view of the matter. He said the fault lay with those who had made use of the figures, in a sense that ProfessoT Shortt did not intend. Then I say he should at once chide his associates on the other side of the House for so quickly taking up, in a time of alleged truce, this statement, shown this afternoon to have been in substance and in fact absolutely false, and passing it on to the country for the truth, when it is not the truth, as I have shown conclusively in connection with my department, and as some of my colleagues have shown conclusively in connection with their departments. I would say that the judicial spirit, a spirit of the most strict and scrupulous impartiality, should be ex-

hibited by 'every member of the Civil Service Commission, because, as in the case of the judiciary, I hold that confidence, the confidence of every one in this House, of both parties, and of the Government and Opposition, confidence in the fairness and impartiality of the members of that tribunal, is the very foundation and basis of its usefulness.
What does the hon. minister think of the suggestion of the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) as to.how this matter should be disposed of?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think over a great number of things that my hon. friend puts forward, and probably he would not mind if I would think over this suggestion also.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intervene in this debate for the purpose of discussing the relative merits of the understanding of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) and of Professor Shortt. The Minister of Public Works was discussing the return of his own department, and, as I understand it, Professor Shortt was discussing the returns of the different departments of the Government. But I would like to say a word respecting the appointments to the inside service and to the outside service, since the right hon. the Prime Minister has given us this opportunity, and we may not have another opportunity this session. But just before entering upon the very few remarks I propose to make, I would like to say to the Minister of Finance that we on this side of the House have always considered him too big a man to make a statement such as he made a few moments ago, when he said that we upon this side of the House do not thoroughly appreciate the gravity of the situation which confronts the Empire. I say that as regards myself, at least, and I am sure as regards every hon. member upon this side of the House, no more dishonourable, no more dishonest, no more unfair statement, Sir, has ever been made in this House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wish to say to the hon. member that the use . of such language is not permissible. He cannot apply such a word as " dishonourable " to a statement made-by a member of the House.
Take it back.

I will take back anything which is against the rules of the House. I am not applying the words to the statement made by the Minister of Finance.
42i
I am saying, Sir, and I repeat, that so far as the statement refers to members of this House, no more dishonourable, no more dishonest, and no more unfair statement could be made.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member cannot evade the rules in an indirect way. By the rules of debate, it is not permissible to impute dishonourable motives to any hon. member in this House.

I submit to your ruling,
Sir, as I always do in this House. I will it vould be dishonourable, dishonest, and unfair for any hon. member of this House to have, upon the subject of the war confronting the British Empire at the present moment, feelings such as the Minister of Finance would have the House believe that hon. gentlemen on this side of House possess. Am I within the rules of the House, Mr. Speaker? I presume the only object of the Minister of Finance in making such a statement was to lead the country to believe that the Opposition, in discussing the Budget or any question which comes before the House, was trying to prevent the Government from carrying out all measures necessary, in their judgment, for the defence of this country. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that we upon this side of the House have as keen a sense of our responsibilities as members of this House as those who have imputed to us such unfair, dishonest and dishonourable conduct. I want to say further, that there are too many men fighting the battles of the motherland on the battlefields of Europe at the present time and directly related to us on this side of the House to allow us to forget for a single moment this awful war, if we had absolutely no other reason to remind us of our duties in this conflict.
I have but a few words to add concerning the Civil Service of this country. At Halifax the right hon. the Premier made the following statement:
A thorough and complete reformation of the laws relating to the Civil Service should be put into effect, so that future appointments shall be made by an independent commission acting upon the report of examiners after competitive examination. I am convinced that we shall perform a great public duty by establishing in this country that system which prevails in Great Britain, under which a member of parliament has practically no voice in or control over any appointment to the Civil Service.
To use the power of filling positions in the public service as a reward for party service and without regard to the character and capacity of the individual selected is a gross

breach of a solemn public trust... A private trustee so dishonouring- his office would be subject to punishment by the criminal law.
When the right hon. Prime Minister made that statement the country believed that he intended to reform the Civil Service. Following that solemn pledge given to the people of this country, the Prime Minister brought from England Sir George Murray. Sir George Murray made a report upon the Civil Service. A great sum of money was spent in connection with the report but no action was taken upon it. Carrying out his pledge still further, the Prime Minister had investigating commissioners appointed throughout the country, to investigate into the acts of civil servants during the campaign of 1911. When the investigating commissioners found that civil servants were taking part in the elections, another step was taken, if not in all cases, at least in some which have come to my attention. The employee was very politely asked for his resignation. If he did not resign he would be dismissed. The employee consequently tendered his resignation under compulsion, knowing'that the alternative would be dismissal. As many Grits as possible were got out of the service in that way, and we now find that to take the place of some two- or four thousand civil servants- I am indifferent as to the figures-some ten or eleven thousand were appointed. Of course it is simply a question of proportion just how many Tories we required to take the place of a Grit. But if three Tories are necessary to take the place of one Grit who has been dismissed, and the country has to pay these three Tories, I think the country will say that it would have been better to leave that Grit in his place, and certainly cheaper for the country.
This patronage question has always been a disturbing one in this country. During some eight years I have had considerable experience in patronage myself, and I know pretty will what I am speaking of. I do not think there is an lion, member upon either side of the House who, if he spoke the truth, would not say that he would like to see patronage abolished. I am not speaking in a carping spirit, and I do not want to attack the Government or to lay any unnecessary blame upon it. I should like to see the Government find some way of remedying the condition of the outside service in this country. I understand that my right hon. friend could not very well place the whole outside service under one central commission. The right hon. gentleman has found fault with what the Liberal party
[Mr. Devlin. 3
have done. We undertook to reform the Civil Service. We began by appointing a commission to deal with the inside service, and in time we would have reached the outside service. But the party which replaced the Liberal party has not yet been able to come before the country and say w'hat they purpose to do to reform this iniquitous system. How well I remember the Minister of Trade and Commerce holding up his hands with horror and saying:	This system of patronage is
iniquitous; you are appointing men to office upon the recommendation of members of Parliament; such a state of things should not exist. Mr. Speaker, I, too, believe that such things should not exist. I feel that if it were possible to deal with the outside service as a great employer deals with his help, it would be a great deal better for the country, and a great deal better for the members supporting the Government. It takes away from the usefulness of a Government supporter to be continually harassed by demands for Government positions. Take the case of the Minister of Public Works. I do not suppose there is a better natured man in the Cabinet than he. But what can he do? A dozen or twenty members get after him for appointments of their friends to the outside service. He would like to refuse, but he cannot; he is too good-hearted. Besides he is not paying the salaries himself; the country pays them. And so he takes on twenty or thirty or forty or a thousand or two thousand. It does not matter to him. Let the country pay. He is a good fellow, and the members will continue to support the Government. The late Postmaster General was even a better natured man than my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, for according to a return brought down he appointed some nine thousand men. / He showed better nature there than I think any man in this House would have given him credit for.
Just a word of recommendation to the Prime Minister in closing? Get busy in connection with the patronage system.	It has given trouble at all
times in this country. It has been reported that during a coalition Government, the Government was upset because the members supporting the Liberal party could not conciliate the Tory end of the Cabinet, and the Tories could not satisfy the Liberal end in the matter of appointments.
I feel that the Prime Minister would like to do something better, and it is now time

6G1
for him to find some way in which to improve the outside service. I am very sorry that at the beginning of my remarks I may have been a little harsher with my lion, friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White) than I had meant to be, but I know that he will not bear me any ill will.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not a bit.
At this critical time in the Empire's history we all have a pretty strong feeling on the question of the war.

Mr., Speaker, as I represent in this House what has been described as the most. offending department of the Government, I desire to say a few words in defence of the administration of the Post Office Department. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Devlin) has said that it appears by the return which was produced here this afternoon that my predecessor made about 9,000 appointments during the three years covered by the return brought down. Although I hold no brief for my predecessor, Hon. L. P. Pelletier, who enjoys the reputation, in this House and in this country, of having been one of the best administrators that ever presided over the Post Office Department, I feel that it is my duty to answer the statement made by the hon. member (Mr. Devlin). I shall give a few figures to show the number of employees in the Post Office Department, and the extent of the business done by the department, during the last three years, which will, I believe, justify the increase in the number of employees. Do hon. gentlemen know that in the department in Ottawa we have over 700 employees, that outside of the department we have 8,000 employees, and that there are over 15,000 postmasters, making a total of about 23,700 employees, and, therefore, if within the last three years 8,000 or 9,000 appointments have been made, it need sui'prise no one. Hon. gentlemen upon the other side of the House will admit that during the greater portion of this period the business of the country was growing by leaps and bounds, and that, under such circumstances, it was not at all strange that 9,000 new appointments should have been made? The Post Office Department is not essentially a revenue producing department; it renders a public service to the country, which, to be effective, and to meet the demands of our modern civilization must be the very best that money can procure. I conceive it to be the duty of the Postmaster General to make our postal service as perfect as possible, and that is the duty I have set before me to discharge,
whether I have a surplus in the department or whether I have a deficit. The post office cannot stand still; it must progress with the progress of Canada.
Let me refer to the reports of the Post Office Department for the last two years. I find in the report of the Postmaster General for the year ended March 31, 1913-
Why not take the report for the year 1914?

I am coming to that, if my hon. friend will possess his soul in patience for one minute; it is a better report than the report for 1913 and I am leaving the choice morsel for the last. The report for 1913 says:
There has been an increase of 2,151 miles in the extent of the system over which mails are carried by railway. The number of miles which mails have been carried by railway and water routes, and ordinary land routes is greater by 2,264,362 miles than it was for the year before.
The estimated increase in the number of letters and post cards sent during the year is
73.252.000,	which is about 11% per cent more than the figures of 1912.
Owing to the growth of the service in the directions mentioned, the expenditure has increased by $1,710,769.10, as compared with last year, but there was a surplus front the operation of the service which amounts to $1,177,671.86.
Then by the report for the year ended March 31, 1914. We find that there was an increase of 350 in the number of post office money order offices, and an increase of 38 in the number of post office savings bank offices. There was an increase of 648 in the number of new post offices which, multiplied by three, for the three years for which the report has been brought down, would give an increase of over 1,800 new post offices, with a corresponding increase in the number of employees in those offices. The report for 1914 says:
There has been an increase of 913 miles in the extent of the system over which the mails are carried by railway. The number of miles which mails have been carried by railway and water routes, and ordinary land routes is greater by 4,278,257 miles than it was for the year before.
The estimated increase in the number of letters and post cards sent during the year is
43.519.000,	which is about 6J per cent more than the figures of 1913.
The number of rural mail delivery routes has been increased by 940, and over 48,000 boxes have been erected on these additional routes.
One must also take into account the establishment of the parcel post, which necessitated the appointment of quite a number of new employees.

1 repeat that the post office service cannot stand still, that it must keep on growing with the country, that an increasing number of employees is necessary to give a good service as the business increases, and that the department and the Government, instead of being blamed, as they have been blamed by hon. gentlemen opposite to-day, should have been eulogized and lauded for what they have done.	*
Let me call your attention to one or two facts. I wonder how many hon. gentlemen have ever been in the post office in the city of Toronto. I visited the post office in Toronto in the month of December last and I was astonished to see the increase in the business of that office and the volume of business carried on there. I observed the businesslike way in which the employees were working and that every employee was absolutely intent upon doing his work and doing it well. Do hon. gentlemen realise that within the last two or three years the business of the Toronto post office has so increased that to-day there is more business being done in the Toronto office than in the post offices in Montreal and in Winnipeg combined? It was incumbent upon the Post Office Department to man the Toronto post office so that that great and enterprising city should have a post office worthy of it. The city of Montreal is increasing in population at the rate of 50,000 a year. Do hon. gentlemen opposite think that the post office service in that growing city should be allowed to stand still? Surely it was good business to keep up with the times and so it was necessary to increase the number of employees in the post office in Montreal during the last two or three years.
Something has been said by my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) as to the report which was brought down and which includes in it the 9,000 employees who appeared to have been appointed during the last three years. I am told by the responsible officers of the department that this figure of 9,000 includes the temporary employees who are appointed for the rush seasons at Christmas and New Nears, and that it includes also the employees whom the Post Office Department is obliged to take on during the summer months when a very considerable number of the ordinary employees are given their holidays. If you take the increased business of the post offices in the great cities into consideration, the establishment of new post offices and new systems, if you remember that in the interests of the whole com-
munity the post office service cannot be allowed to stand still while the country is making progress, and if you take into consideration the further fact that the number which is mentioned in that report embraces not only all the employees who have been appointed permanently but the temporary employees also, you must come to the conclusion that as to the Post Office Department we are able confidently to come before Parliament to justify our policy.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Customs):
speechtext:
I do not wish to prolong this debate; but as Professor Shortt has paid a little attention to my department, I feel that it would not be fair to that department to let this discussion close without making a few remarks. The remarks of Professor Shortt that apply to my department are comprised in this short statement:
Professor Shortt asked:	" Who took the
places of the 2,000 civil servants who were reported in the House the other day to have been dismissed from the service?" His reply to his own question was, " Just 10,000."
In the return submitted from my department, the question was asked: How many dismissals? The answer was: 271. In addition to that there was question No. 2: How many resignations? The answer was: 194 resignations. Professor Shortt, in his statement, never referred to the resignations; and therefore, as far as the Customs is concerned, I do not hesitate to say that his statement was false and untrue and dishonest in every shape and form. I also do not hesitate to say, knowing Professor Shortt, that the statement was made deliberately for the purpose of influencing the electorate of this country politically against this Government.

What does the
hon. member know about Professor Shortt to make him believe that this statement was deliberately dishonest?
Deliberately dishonest because he did not include some of the answers in the return brought down.

That is not answering
my question. The minister says his knowledge of Professor Shortt led him to the conclusion that that statement was deliberately dishonest.

Professor Shortt, before he
became Chairman of the Civil Service Commission, was a bitter politician, and from that time forward I have never learned that he has changed in that respect.
Then, are all politicians or men interested in politics dishonest?

Certainly not. I would not
for one moment make that charge.
That is what you say.

I wish to state that if any
man is appointed to and continues in a Government position, if he uses it for political purposes, he is dishonest.
I would not for one moment attribute anything unfair to the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), but I rose more particularly to correct a statement which he made, because I fear that it may go to the public and they may believe him where they will not believe Professor Shortt. I do not wish to evade the
rule of the House, but I wish to say that I have heard the hon. junior 9 p.m. member for Halifax make the statement that a return brought down in this House showed that there were 271 dismissals and 1,659 appointments. When he made that statement, I claim that in fairness to the Customs Department he should have stated also that the return showed 271 dismissals and 194 resignations. In other words, he made the same mistake as Professor Shortt did when he was making his speech in Ottawa on that Sunday evening. It was unfair to the Customs Department for the junior member for Halifax to let a statement of that kind go to the public from this House. If I did not take this opportunity of correcting his statement it would not be fair to my department.
At the time I made the statement, I did not know about the resignations.
I take that answer as correct; but if I remember aright the hon. member's statement, he said he had a return that justified that statement.

Does the hon. member
know the number of desertions in his department?

gaged them all the way up to seventy-five or eighty years of' age, putting men into the service who were absolutely of no use whatever. After getting into power the Liberals thought it would be better to have a commission with Professor Shortt as chairman. Professor Shortt has ability, there is no doubt about that; but he certainly was a politician and a good one for the Liberal party. He started out to reform the Civil Service, and he was going to show how he could improve it by means of examinations. If I want a customs officer to-day, I have to get one who will answer questions, samples of which I will give. And when I quote these questions, I would like to know if there is a man in this House, from the right hon. gentleman who leads the House, down to the humblest member, who can answer them. If we want a locker, simply a man to open cases, etc., a labouring man, he has to pass an examination and to get a certain proportion of marks in each subject. For instance, he has to know a little about geography, so he is supposed to answer this question:
In what sections of Canada is lumbering an important industry? Where does the lumber for each section find a market?
From what places in western Europe do Canadians get silk, cotton goods, woollens, oranges, steel ?
Are not those proper questions relating to the customs ? l

They are not improper if you can get a man to answer them. But I venture to say the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) could not answer them himself. Now, if I want a clerk, he has to be able to answer some questions in history such as the following:
What were the Crusades? When did they take place? Name some important events connected with them.
Give an account of the French revolution of 1791, as follows: (a) Causes; (b) Prominent men who took part; (c) Important events.
He must know something of grammar, of course, and so he is asked to parse each italicised word and phrase in an extract which is given. And he is virtually told: If you cannot parse these words you cannot get into the Customs service.
Cannot parse.

Here are more questions in geography:
Where do the people of Great Britain and Ireland obtain the raw materials for the manufacture of silk, tobacco, cotton, woollen and leather goods?

Compare the climate of Manitoba with that of England. What natural conditions cause the difference?
Perhaps I ought not to give more for fear of making the whole Civil Service look ridiculous. But let me give one or two questions in arithmetic:
A person watches a train and finds that it takes 17 seconds to pass him. The train is 374 feet long. At what rate in miles per hour is the train travelling?
A starts on a journey at the rate of 3 miles an hour; 6 hours afterwards B starts after him at the rate of 4 miles an hour. How far will B travel before he overtakes A?
How many days will it take 30 men to do a piece of work which 20 men can do in 45 days ?
Now, let me give a few figures as to my own department. In the inside service, in October, 1911, we had 198 employees, and in January of this year we had 232 employees, an increase of 34. In the outside service, I admit, there has been a large increase. We had 2,273 officers in October, 1910-11, and 3,144 in January, 1914-15, an increase of 871. But let me point out that our revenue for 1911 was $73,312,367.50, while in 1914 our customs revenue was $107,179,360.33. In
1910-11 we had customs entries to the number of 1,387,310 inwards and 404,664 outwards. In 1913-14 we bad 1,898,110 inwards and 507,224 outwards, or, in round numbers half a million more entries inwards and a hundred thousand more outwards.
Like the appointments- more inward than outward.

There was good reason for every appointment made. The hon. member for South Renfrew knows, perhaps better than anybody else, the policy of his own party when they came into power. He knows that they dismissed every man on the St. Lawrence canals and then put on the same number as had been formerly employed.
But there were not half so many as there are now.
There are no more on the canals now than there were when the Liberals turned these men out.
Not in winter time.

Talking of the winter time, when the Liberal party was in power they spent $35,000 in keeping the canals lighted, though they were all frozen up. I have shown that in my department there was a Very large increase.
What is the revenue up to the first of the present month?
I have not those figures before me, but I am very glad to be able to tell the hon. member that the revenue for last month was about $250,000 higher than for the same month last year.
And the war still on?

So far as the increase in the number of employees is concerned, the Customs Department is in the same position as the Post Oflice Department. We have opened some 54 new outports. We have had demands from the collectors of the large ports-Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Victoria and other important centres- for more employees; we have not appointed any more officials than the collectors and inspectors reported to be absolutely necessary. I think it will be agreed that in view of the large increase in revenue, very many morei officials were required. The people will know, from the statements of fact that have been made from time to time in this House, that we were justified in increasing the number of employees in the Department of Customs. I rose not particularly to explain this phase of the question, but to correct the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) and to point out that the assertions that I heard him make in this House are not in accordance with the return that was brought down. The people will know, therefore, that the statement made by the hon. member cannot be accepted as a justifiable charge against the Customs Department.
Having regard to the utterances of Prof. Shortt, I care very little what assertions go forth in respect of my department. We all know what he is politically; we all know what he would do so far as the Civil Service and the Government are concerned. I believe that Prof. Shortt's statements were made deliberately to injure the Government, and I feel that after making those statements he is not entitled to very much consideration from this House, from the Government, or from the people of Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton):
speechtext:
There are a number of reasons
why I should take part in this debate, but the chief one is that I could not resist the temptation to take advantage of the inspiration which would be afforded me by following the very excellent discourse which we have received from the Minister of Customs on the educational development
of this country. I consider it a great pity that a man like the Minister of Customs should be obliged to devote himself to adding up columns of figures and worrying about customs houses and that sort of thing when the educational development of Canada is in need of his assistance. I endeavoured to follow him in the remarks which he made-I am an old school teacher -but in many respects he was a little too swift for me. I thought I would have some fun with him on the question of parsing, but he carefully avoided that subject; I do not think he is particularly fond of parsing. He kept away from analysis, too; analysis was never his forte. I have listened to his speeches in this House for the last 10 or 12 years, and I am in a position to say that, they certainly would not stand much analysis. His composition is heresy of the first water; his theology is blasphemy. If there is any method by which the Prime Minister can make a shuffle in the Cabinet and have some one else take the position of Minister of Customs, I would advise him to do so, thus giving the country the benefit of my hon. friend's services as an educationalist-* because that is his proper sphere.
The hon. minister was wont in the course of his remarkk to discard almost everything as being too difficult. I wonder if he would permit us to discard certain difficult portions of the multiplication table. When I was learning the multiplication table I remember that seven times nine times were regarded as exceedingly difficult; perhaps the riiinister would, in his capacity as educationalist, direct his efforts towards having these portions of the multiplication table discarded. My hon. friend's attitude reminds me forcibly of the story of the negro who had three things to look after, two blast furnaces and a locomotive. Reporting in the morning, he said: The fires in the furnaces burned out and they were useless all night, and the locomotive was out of order; otherwise, everything was all right. The minister was coming down the scale so rapidly and throwing away everything as he came along' that I thought he was not going to approve of anything. It would seem that the babe as he came from the cradle is the kind of officer my hon. friend wants "for his department.
As to history, my hon. friend no doubt appreciates the fact that the history of the Tory party would be exceedingly embarrassing. As to geography, why should a Tory know where he is or where he is going? In respect of ordinary mathematics, particularly with regard to the cost of

things, the minister and his friends do not bother their heads very much. These things are all very embarrassing to my hon. friend; all defences-if the Prime Minister will pardon my referring to a stale legal phrase-are embarrassing. I would suggest that the Prime Minister give the Minister of Customs a free hand, and let him adopt as his ideal the style of education which Adam had when he was fresh from the hands of the Creator. I should like to find out from my hon. friend the kind of syllabus that he would prepare for submission to the high educationalists of the province of Ontario. So much for the question of education.
I know enough about the Prime Minister to believe that he would like to give everybody a fair show and a fair trial. I do not believe that the atmosphere with which he is now surrounded would change his attitude in that respect. The right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition has brought up a question which involves affording a gentleman who holds a high office in this country, a servant of the people, an opportunity of defending himself and of explaining his position. This high court of Parliament is not open to him; his position is such that he cannot very well defend himself on the platform. He has no right to ask a minister of the Government or anybody else in this House to meet him on the hustings for the purpose of discussing the matter, and he is, therefore, shut out from the ordinary means of defence which are open to other persons. I think, therefore, that it is but fair and proper that the right hon. leader of the Opposition should bring this matter to the attention of the House. I am sorry to find that the matter was dealt with in such a harsh and turbulent manner by hon. gentlemen on the Government side of the House.
I observed to-day that the Minister of Marine was running at very high tension and on very high gear shortly after he commenced speakiug. When the Minister of Marine has only very poor grist the mill goes at a tremendous rate of speed, the wheels sound very high; and I should not wish for any better evidence of very poor substance and very poor grist for his mill than the speed at which he was going to-day. He had nothing, and so it was like him to pour a continuous tirade of abuse on this man Shortt, who is not here to defend himself. I submit, with all candour, that I do not think it is an evidence of bravery on the part of big men to get absolutely fortified within the walls of this House, and, t under the privileges which are theirs by 
reason of being members of Parliament, abuse a poor fellow who is tied hand and foot and cannot answer for himself. I am pleased to know that there was' not very much of a case made out against this man Shortt. The awful noise that was made about his mis-statement turns out in this way: He says that 10,000 men were appointed anew by this Administration, within the last few years, over and above filling every office that fell vacant by any of the different ways by which vacancies occur. A return was brought down, or a calculation made from a return, which shows that not only
8.000	or 10,000 but 11,000 appointments were made, after providing for every resignation and every dismissal. That is the statement made by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) as I understand it. That is not all. There are some departments yet to be heard from. If it is true, and it is from the records of the different departments, that
11.000	extra appointments have been made oyer and above the number in office when this Government came into power, what is the trouble over the statement made by Professor Shortt? It reminds me of an old man I once knew who made a great fuss because some one said he was twenty pounds in debt. He said it was scoundrelly, rascally, and unfair- I am now following the vocabulary of the Minister of Marine-that he was not twenty pounds in debt. He was asked what his debt was, and he said it was not twenty pounds; it was 19 pounds, 19 shillings, and tuppence, which was just a half penny short of the twenty pounds. Even if Professor Shortt said that 10,000 had been appointed, what is the fuss about? He said 10,000 or 8,000, and we find 11,000 new men appointed. If that is true, why should there be such a fuss about it? It is simply proving that perhaps Prof. Shortt did not make his statement exactly in a way that would suit hon. gentlemen, but when it is all boiled down, when you come down to the hard facts, to brass tacks as the saying is, if $11,000,000 must be provided this year over the amount provided in 1911 to pay for the Civil Service, and only to provide for new appointments, there is no particular fault to be found with Professor Shortt except that he made that statement publicly. It has been said here that this man is a narrow partisan. I never so understood from any one I have talked with. I have not the honour of his acquaintance, but members beside me speak of him as rather an austere man,

who would not give way to anybody, who held opinions of his own and would not give them up. The first time I ever heard of him in Nova Scotia was when he was selected as chairman of a board of conciliation by the other members of the board, who agreed that- he was a man eminently fair and just, and suitable to preside over a board to bring about a settlement of a labour dispute. From that day to this I have never heard of him as being a narrow partisan. However, be that as it may, I hope he will get justice at the hands of the Government, and if there is any defence necessary that he shall be given the fullest opportunity of making it.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries was very austere this afternoon about members of the Civil Service or any one who was receiving money from the Government for services, doing anything but just properly earning the salary paid to them. I wish to see how he is carrying out this austere system in his own department. I wish to know if he has kept his officers in the department over which he so ably presides right down to the rule which he laid down for Professor Shortt. Last winter, from my place in this House, I asked him- if a certain man in Nova Scotia, named Fraser, residing in Queens county, was an officer in his department. He told me that he was an officer in his department. I find this winter that he is still an officer in his department. I find that in February last he was an officer in his department, and when he should have been looking after the affairs of his office and earning money for the minister, where do I find him ? I find him away down in the extreme northern part of the province of Nova Scotia, in the county of Victoria, electioneering. And what is said about him ? A certain trial took place down there, and a certain judge of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia made certain findings, one of them being:
The following persons have, in my judgment, been proven at the trial to have been guilty of corrupt practices in this election,
Then he gives a long string of names. In that string is the servant of my hon. friend, W. E. Fraser, of Liverpool, Queens county, N.S. In that list the judge finds twenty-three men, exactly in the same category as the representative of my hon. friend the minister, and he finds them all guilty under the same charge. I submit to all the members of the Government, that not less than seventy-five per cent of that list are officials of this Government, men who
are in the pay of this Government, who had gone out of their offices and so conducted themselves that this judge, who is certainly not anxious to find harsh things, unless he has to, finds twenty-three of them guilty, and so says in his judgment. This very matter was brought to the notice of the minister about a year ago, but he has never made the slightest inquiry as to how this man Fraser was attending to his business. He is .still in the pay of the Government and will continue to be, and his salary will probably be raised owing to his useful ser vices in the elections. That is only a sample of the way that public servants are basking in the sunshine of this Administration, knowing that the more they do in the way of political rascalities, the better they will be paid and the better they will be liked.
There is another matter which, in justice to myself, it is_ obligatory on me to bring to. the notice of the House. I am particularly pleased that the Minister of Customs is in his seat, because, despite his regard for care and fairness, he has lately been exceedingly unfair to myself.
I see by yesterday's Hansard that he says that a certain statement I made in this House last year is untrue. I take it, Mr. Speaker, that I am permitted to look at last year's Hansard, and that I am not violating any rule in doing so. It was rather a strong thing for the Minister to say that I made a false statement, without ever asking me, who am a member of thiB House, whether the statement was false or not. If I made a statement in this House, and the minister in answering a question found it necessary to settle a question of fact one way or the other, I think under those circumstances a member of this House can expect to be given an opportunity of stating how he understood the facts before a minister undertakes to say, without ever consulting the member, that his statement is false. The question I am referring to appears on page 646 of Hansard, and was asked yesterday by the hon. member for Guysborough. The question was in respect to the services of Mr. Duchemin, who has been in the service of the Government for the greater part of the last two years. It has been found that that gentleman received last year money out of the coffers of this country to the extent of something like $6,380.48, and it is only fair that we who are to some extent responsible to the people should make inquiry as to how he earned that money. Last year, in my place in this

House, when the Estimates of the Minister of Public Works were going through, I made a statement which appears on page 5238 of last year's Hansard, and with your permission, Mr. Speaker, and in justice to myself, I am obliged to read the very short statement that I made on that occasion. I wish to read it with a view to showing that what I said about Mr. Duchemin, who is a servant of this country, was in my judgment absolutely correct then, and is ahsolutoJv correct now; aud when the minister undertook, in answering a question, to make the bald statement that I did not state the truth, I submit that he was in error and did not fully inquire into the facts. This is what I said when this matter was up last year:
Mr. McKenzie:	I wish to refer briefly to investigations 'held under the Inquiries Act. In Nova Scotia we had headsmen in each county, sometimes one headsman for more than one county. In North Cape Breton and Victoria, in fact all the counties of Cape Breton and eastern Nova Scotia, we had a commissioner named Duchemin, who was a very active commissioner. I understand that the Orders in Council appointing those commissioners fixed their salaries at $15 dollars a day with incidentals, and they only received $15 no matter how many inquiries they conducted in one day. Mr. Duchemin is a man of my own profession, a barrister of some standing, a strong temperance advocate, a man who stands high in his church, and besides all his other virtues he is the editor of the Tory organ, the Sydney Post, in the city of Sydney. Being a prominent man and always preaching righteousness and truthfulness and honesty through his paper and on the platform, it strikes one as peculiar that there should be anything but the most rigid particularity and punctuality about anything that he would do. A man of such high standing would be expected to be very particular when he would come to deal with money matters in which he was personally interested, and where his own personal interests were put in contradistinction to those of the country. On September 6, 1912, Mr. Duchemin held court at a place called Big Bras D'Or in the county of Victoria. He there examined Captain George Livingstone, Captain Roderick McDonald, D. J. Morrison and H. G. McKay, Roderick Bain and Roderick McLeod. These investigations were held between 3 p.m. and 6 p.m. Under the Order in Council Mr. Duchemin would be entitled to $15 for the afternoon's services, besides his travelling expenses, etc. But I find that he submitted to the department six different bills with a full charge in every one of the bills, charging for that afternoon $128.95, while $20 would be about what he was entitled to. The items of the accounts, six of which are exactly alike, are as follows:
To travel, issuing notices, subpoenas,
etc., conducting inquiries	..	..	$15.00" Allowance for living	expenses	....	2.50' Perry fare	05" Horse hire	1,00
" Paid for use of room for holding
inquiries	40
" Service of witnesses	 1.00

To Stenographer copying evidence and
reports	 $	1.35
" Stationary and postage	05

That is the alleged expenditure, Mr. Speaker, in connection with only one inquiry, and that is all that you have been charged for, what took place at Bras D'Or on that day. The Hansard report goes on: The account in McKay's case is as follows:
Allowance	 $15.00
Living allowance	 3.00
Witnesses, typewriting	 5.40
Total	$23.10
You will observe, Mr. Speaker, that his dinner in the first instance only cost him $2.50. The same day he bought another dinner for $3, and there is a similar item in each of the six bills, so he took six dinners on the same day, and crossed the ferry five times to examine witnesses, when as a matter of fact there was only one sole, solitary inquiry, at which all the witness were examined in less than one hour and a half, and the proper charge for which was $21.35. The Hansard report goes on:
These accounts cover the six cases that were tried upon the same day, totalling $128.95, whereas ' $21.20 would have been the proper charge. The .men who were investigated and finally dismissed were my political friends, and I was keeping tab on this inquiry. I knew the day on which it was to be held, but to make absolutely sure I wrote to Captain McDonald asking him about this Investigation. He writes me from Bras d'Or on the 10th March, 1913, as follows:
Big Bras d'Or, Cape Breton,
March 10, 1913.
D. D. McKenzie, M.P.,
Ottawa, Canada.
My dear friend,-Yours to hand of the 8th instant, and in reply would say you are quite correct as to the date of the investigation. It was held on September 6, at three o'clock p.m., the whole being done between three and six o'clock p.m. The names of the parties who were investigated are as follows: George Livingston, sub-collector; Rod. McDonald, preventive officer; Rory Bain, D. J. Morrison, and Rod. McLeod, boatman; and H. C. McKay, lightkeeper, Bird island.
All those were investigated on the one afternoon at the time before mentioned.
On that occasion I pointed out to the Minister of Public Works that these things were absolutely correct then, and they are absolutely correct now. For an investigation of two and a half hours, this man, who was a servant of this Government, charged $128.95, when he should have charged $21.
The answer in yesterday's Hansard about which I am complaining is as follows

-Mr. Coderre answering for the Customs Department:
The charge made by the member for North Cape Breton was looked into by Customs Department and inquired into by -Auditor General and found to be not true.
I submit to the minister that it is true, absolutely true, and I challenge his inquiry. I care not what the Minister of Customs may think of rpe, but I do think a great deal of my own veracity. I have been in this House for a great many years, and I am getting somewhat of an old man now to be told I go around this country peddling falsehoods against anybody. I challenge the minister or anybody else to point out where I ever made a statement on the floor of this House that was not absolutely correct. I submit that it is the duty of the minister who put on the records of the Parliament of this country against me that I made an untrue statement, to make inquiry and to apologize to me for making a statement which was not true. I say that that money was taken for an investigation and for services where it was not earned. I did not say it was embezzlement, I did not say it was theft; I did not characterize it at all. Before I made my statement I had asked the minister what the Order in Council allowed this man, and he told me it was $15 a day. I have not the Hansard under my hand but that is my recollection. It is well known that he was to get $15 a day no matter whether he made one inquiry or a dozen, or made no inquiry at all, but it was not the intention that, if he spent an hour or two and met with half a dozen or twenty people, he should send a bill in for each one, as was done in this case. I stand by the facts as shown by the record. I got the facts from the department. I moved for the returns, they were brought down and I have them in my possession. These are not my figures, but they are the figures of the department, and without the same testimony, without knowing the facts, the Minister of Customs comes down and says that a member of this House makes a false statement. I protest that when such things as these are said in the face of hon. members in the House who are able to defend themselves, it is not surprising to know what is said about Prof. Shortt, whose hands are tied and whose tongue cannot be used in his own defence in this House. I could not permit this to pass over without bringing it to the notice of the House. It is a duty between one member and another to protect the honour of members of this House, and
no hon. member should be permitted to be put on record as being a falsifier when the facts do not bear out-this accusation. These ate the facts as I have stated them, these records were before the Minister of Customs when he made this statement, and I may say that 1 would not have noticed his statement at all had it not been called to my notice by an hon. gentleman. With reference to the record of Mr. Duchemin, the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) was asked by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair):
Does the minister intend to investigate the conduct of Mr. Duchemin?
Mr. Hazen:	X have no such intention.
There is put before the hon. gentlemen who are responsible for the expenditure of the moneys of this country the record and conduct of one of their servants; they are asked: Do you propose to inquire into his conduct-and a responsible minister says: I have no such intention.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. W. FOWLER (Kings and Albert):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is an old saying that all roads lead at last to Rome. Everything that the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) debates leads at last to Duchemin. The hon. member for North Cape Breton, who is sometimes quite witty and amusing, but at other times, oh, so doleful, and dreadfully dull and prosy, has, during the last three years, taken part in a good many debates; and, even if the subject matter was as far removed from Duchemin, or anything appertaining to him, as the poles are asunder, the hon. gentleman, with that peculiar cast of mind which works in subterranean and intricate passages, always comes back at last to Duchemin. Talk about the proverbial red rag to the male animal of the ox gender; that is not a circumstance to the name of Duchemin to the ex-judicial member for North Cape Breton. The hon. gentleman was very witty in the first portion of his speech, very amusing, but he did not amuse anybody half so much as he did himself. He enjoyed his time-worn, stale, moth-bitten jokes much more than anybody else did. Even the admiring chorus of back-

benchers had to take second place to the hon. gentleman himself in that respect. The hon. gentleman told us that he was once a schoolmaster. We could have guessed that. He must have been for many years a schoolmaster and got into that narrow pedantic groove that schoolmasters sometimes fall into. But if we are to judge of the rest of his scholastic knowledge by the sample of arithmetic which he gives us, we must come to the conclusion that he was a very poor schoolmaster indeed and that he taught his pupils very badly. He told us that 19 pounds 19 shillings and tuppence-which is short for two pence- was within a half penny of twenty pounds.
I will make the correction now. I meant 19 pounds, 19 shillings and 11 pence halfpenny.

Too late; too late-you
have lost your ninepence ha'penny. Your pupils would be reduced to poverty if they followed your instructions in arithmetic. My hon. friend has spoken of Mr. Shortt, and very shortly of Mr. Shortt, but at considerable length of Mr. Duchemin. I do not propose to discuss the Duchemin question now. That has been discussed on several occasions, and I have no doubt that if the hon. gentleman ever meets Mr. Duchemin on a platform in any portion of Nova Scotia Mr. Duchemin will be able to take care of the hon. member for North Cape Breton. He speaks of Mr. Shortt as being a poor martyr who was tongue-tied. It would have been much better for Shortt if he had been tongue-tied. The trouble with Shortt is that he was not tongue-tied at all. He got himself into this trouble; he began it, and not with the statement the hon. member for Cape Breton said he made. I would have thought that when a man had for two or three years occupied a position upon the judicial bench of this country, and had worn the judicial ermine, he would have acquired some fairness of thought, some impartiality; but the hon. gentleman was just as destitute of that when he came off the bench as he was when he went on it. The hon. gentleman knows that he did not state the actual facts when he gave us his paraphrase of what was said. I will read for the benefit of the hon. gentleman, for he needs all the benefits that can come to him, what Mr. Shortt is reported actually to have said; and remember that Mr. Shortt has never to this moment denied what he did say. Therefore, we must judge him by the record. Some one has said that we should not judge him by newspaper re-
[Mr. Fowler. 2
ports; but if he does not deny these newspaper reports when the opportunity is given him, if, on the contrary, he glories in what he has said, it is not unfair, unreasonable, or unjust to judge him by the newspaper reports. He says:
" I have met men in the Canadian Civil Service," he said, " who, though they held positions under the Government, were quite ready to admit that the Civil Service system was rotten." Professor Shortt asked who took the place of the 2,000 civil servants who were reported in the House the other day to have been dismissed from the service, and his reply to his own question was just "10,000."
Who took the place of the 2,000? 10,000 men took the place of the 2,000. That is what Shortt says. Could language be plainer? In the English language could you put a proposition more plainly than that? Prof. Shortt meant what he said when he' said it, and he knew he was not speaking by the book when he said it. He knew that he was making a statement that was not correct when he said that 10,000 men took the places occupied by the 2,000 men that had been dismissed. That is the fault we find with Prof. Shortt. Tongue-tied! A martyr! Held up in this House to public derision and public shame! Like a lamb before his shearers, is dumb, he could not open his mouth! He is a brave man is Prof. Shortt. I will show you whether he is a brave man or not. If he had been an employee of this Government, subject to be dismissed from office for partisan conduct, and if he had made such a statement, I would say, however improper or unwise his statement was, it had at least the merit of being a bold one, because he took his business life in his hands when he made it. But- what is the situation so far as Prof. Shortt is concerned? He was appointed under an Act which requires the joint action of both Houses of Parliament to dismiss him. He makes this statement. The Senate-that body upon the other side of the building. I look up and see some of the senators in the gallery. Gaze upon the faces in the front row up there-
Mr. SPEAKER-Order. It is not permissible to refer disrespectfully to the Senate.
