You are not a mind reader, Mr. Speaker. How could you possibly know what I was going to say? What have I said that is disrespectful?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The rules of debate prohibit reference to the other branch of this Parliament in a disrespectful or an ironical way. The hon. member was leading on, although he had not gone that

far, to a point where he was likely to be out of order, and I thought it proper to call his attention to the fact.

I was going to speak in the most commendatory terms of the gentlemen sitting in the front row of the gallery. Mr. Speaker, you entirely misapprehend me. I was going to say what firm looking gentlemen they were; how when their minds were once made up to anything, they could not be changed, and that a strong majority of them were in favour of Professor Shortt. I would not say anything derogatory of the Senate. Perhaps I would like to be a senator myself some day, and surely I would not say anything derogatory of that most honourable body.
Shame.
It is a good thing that it has come to you at last.
Mr. Speaker-
Oh, that is the man, is it?
That is where my hon. friend is wrong as usual. I was not the man. I did not say a word.
Then why did my hon. friend get up? I did not name him and I did not point to him.
I never said a word at all.
When the shoe pinches we usually squeal.
You have a suspicious mind, that is all.

Our volcanic friend is erupting again. When Professor Shortt made that utterance he knew that the Senate would not consent to put him out of business for making a statement that would reflect upon the Government of the day. Therefore it was a cowardly act; and to represent him as a man that has been abused and vilified by the gentlemen on this side who have spoken concerning him, is to make a statement that is not in accordance with fact. Professor Shortt has been too kindly and too well used. He deserves much more severe castigation than he has received. A man occupy-10 p.m. ing the position he occupies is supposed to be as impartial and judicial as a judge upon the bench in recommending men for public office, and to show the narrow, bigoted partisanship that Professor Shortt has shown, reveals that
he is absolutely and utterly unworthy of the high office to which he has been appointed.
I am very sorry that the hon. member for St. John city (Mr. Pugsley) is not in his place. During the few moments this evening when I was absent from the House, the hon. gentleman referred to a matter regarding my county. I do not say that he did it intentionally in my absence. I do not quite know how he dragged it in, and I do not see what it has to do with the dereliction of Prof. Shortt, or with the utterances which he made one Sunday night when he should have been at church. My hon. friend said that there had been erected in the county of Kings, which I have the honour to represent, and which gave birth to that distinguished statesman the hon. member for St. John city-although I have never seen on the part of the inhabitants of that beautiful county any particular show of elation on account of that county having been the birthplace of that eminent statesman
Clever!

Another hon. member in pain over there. The statement my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) made regarding the public building at Hampton is altogether beside the fact. He misrepresented the population of the town. He misrepresented the amount of business carried on there. I am very sorry that my hon. friend is not here, because I am surprised that he would make such a statement about the county town of his native county.
My hon. friend also, as I am informed, stated that this was not the proper way in which to bring up this matter with regard to Prof. Shortt; that Prof. Shortt should be brought to the bar of the House; that this method of procedure was unfair and improper. Knowing the admiration that my hon. friend has for his leader, I am surprised that he should make such a statement, because it was his leader who brought this, matter up. The hon. gentleman has had some experience himself with regard to matters of this kind. Let us see what he has done. Did he feel sorry, when he was lashing a certain gentleman, to think that that gentleman had not an opportunity to reply? Did that cause him to restrain his rage? No. A commission once sat in the province of New Brunswick investigating matters in connection with the Central railway. At the head of that commission was one of the most eminent jurists that the province of New Brunswick has produced, a man of high character, of unblemished

reputation, a man who has never stained with one blot the ermine which he wears.
I refer to the Hon. Chief Justice Landry, of New Brunswick. And because the Hon. Chief Justice Landry had the temerity to bring in a report supported by the evidence, absolutely, unqualifiedly supported by the evidence which condemned the conduct of the lion, member for St. John city, he abused, and vilified and lashed the Chief Justice in this House -where that gentleman had no opportunity to reply. Yet he finds it a horrible thing that this ex-schoolmaster, Professor Shortt, should have his conduct characterized, even in the moderate way in which it was characterized by the Hqn. Minister of Public Works. I am surprised, knowing my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works so well, that he restrained himself so much when he had such great provocation. I must not forget my genial friend from Bed Deer (Mr. Clark). He is an angel of peace; he says: Let there be truce, and-there is truce. Let me give something of what he said on the 8th of February last:
The most violent form of partisan strife that can possibly be instigated in any country is a. general election. I think everybody will agree that partisan discussion is at its best in a general election-or at its worst. Perhaps I ought to correct that: Perhaps it finds a lower level still in the literature that is issued prior to an election.
With that premise he makes out that the issuing of this partisan literature is worse, so far as bitterness is concerned, even than the discussion that takes place during the progress of the campaign. Well, if he is thinking of Grit literature, I should be inclined to agree with him; I think scarcely anybody will dispute the position he takes. He told us also in that connection, that with regard to literature: *
I want to claim before this House and the country that we on this side have an absolutely clean sheet. From the moment the war broke out the Bureau was closed,
Beferring now to the bureau for the dissemination of noxious literature tu persons of the Liberal persuasion throughout Canada,
So far as I am concerned, I have never seen a document emanate from it since that time, of a party nature or of any other nature.
1 am sure the hon. gentleman wishes to be fair.
Certainly.

Of course, he will, see that I previously defined the literature as party

literature. I did not need to repeat that phrase at every step.

That is exactly what I
am speaking about. I am going to be absolutely fair to my hon. friend, fairer even than the Minister of Public Works. The hon. member for Bed Deer goes further:
I have never seen a document emanate from it since that time, of a party nature or of any other nature. Where is the laugh of my hon. friends now? Can they produce a leaflet or a document? Not a single one. And I should be wanting in common manliness if I did not assert it.
Now, I am going to ask the hon. gentleman to take that all back. I know that he is a manly gentleman and I am satisfied that when I hold up to his gaze these printed documents, issued between the time war was declared and the time he made his speech, he will withdraw his statement. I hear an hon. gentleman say that this is not party literature. It is called " The Canadian Liberal Monthly ". Let us find the October number, issued soon after the war broke out. We were all standing together shoulder to shoulder like the boys of the old brigade, heart beating close to heart in common defence of the Empire. That was the position we were supposed to occupy. I believe the hon. member for Bed Deer was honest in his view, I believe that he was in earnest and that he was genuine. But what says this delectable sheet, this monthly effusion? How was it keeping the truce? I understand that it is issued once a month; which, perhaps is not unnatural seeing that it is a monthly. And under whose direction is it issued ? That of the right hon. leader of the Opposition, a gentleman who has been spoker. of as a chivalrous man, the wearer of the white plume. Let us see what this says: " A question for Mr. Foster," in big, black type. That refers to Sir George E. Foster, one of the brightest minds in this House, and Minister of Trade and Commerce in this Administration. And this " Question for Mr. Foster " is this:
The French Government has just placed an order with a Pittsburgh firm for enough horseshoe nails to keep that firm going night and day for eighteen months. The Italian Government has just placed an order with a United States firm for $5,000,000 worth of saddles, boots and other leather goods. The Australian Government has just placed an order in the United States for a huge consignment of steel rails. Ail these goods could have been made quite as quickly and as cheaply and of equal quality in Canada. This question suggests itself -Is the Department of Trade and Commerce at

Ottawa doing anything or nothing to guide ord rs from friendly or allied Governments into Canadian channels?
I hear an hon. gentleman say: "No politics in that." Oh, no desire to injure the Government in that. Another fond delusion shattered. I see the hon. member for Red Deer shaking his head as he says: "No politics in that." I thought the hon. member would become indignant as soon as I read this. I should not have expected anything better from the hon. member immediately behind him, but I should have expected something better from the usually chivalrous member for Red Deer.

Would the hon. member allow a question in order to elucidate this matter ? Is it not a fact that the Minister of Trade and Cdmmeree in the documents emanating from his department show's that he is doing his utmost to get trade for Canada out of the war ? And if that be the fact, does my hon. friend think he is guilty of partisanship in doing so ? Or is he showing Canadian patriotism ?
I remember that the father of " my Uncle Toby " was once asked a very pecurliar question-
Never mind vour Uncle Toby.

-a very peculiar question, which had as little bearing upon the subject under , consideration as the question just asked by the hon. member for Red Deer has upon the matter which we are now discussing.
Could anything be more strongly partisan than an attempt to hold up to the execration of the people of Canada the Minister of Trade and Commerce and his department? Was it not partisan to allege that the minister was not doing his duty; that the department was not doing its duty to the f Canadian people, who are making great sacrifices for the Empire; that contracts from foreign countries were, by reason of the supineness of the Department of Trade and Commerce, allowed to go to the United States? Does the hon. member for Red Deer consider that there is nothing of a partisan character in these allegations? In Tespect of all these books, pamphlets and monthlies, the same state of affairs exists. We find that during the time when this truce was supposed to be in operation, this literature was being circulated all over the country. I am sure that this was done without the knowledge of the hon. member foT Red Deer, but I am sorry that I w'as 43 *
mistaken in-assuming that he would admit that this was wrong, and a violation of the truce.

I would if I
knew it to be the case.

No man is so hard to convince as the man who does not wish to be convinced, and I am afraid the hon. gentleman does not wish to be convinced. But, to return to Prof. Shortt for a moment. Prof. Shortt forgot to tell his auditors on that fateful Sunday night-fateful for him-that in the very department over which he presides there have been two dismissals and resignations, and that eight persons have been appointed to take the places of these officials. This is but another instance of Prof. Shortt's unfairness in regard to these matters. The return says that in respect of the Civil Service Commission there were no dismissals, one resignation, one transfer to another department, no desertions from the service, no punishments, and eight appointments to fill two	vacanciesa proportion of four to one. That was keeping up the average pretty well; why did not Professor Shortt be fair enough to make this known? This gentleman is deserving of the condemnation of this House and of this country, and he will receive it when the facts are known by all impartial people. He is deserving of more; if he gets his deserts he will be dismissed from the service of this country by joint address of the House of Commons and of the Senate of Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. J. HUGHES (Kings, Prince Edward Island):
speechtext:
The discussion of this subject has taken a very wide range and several subjects have been brought up which are not quite germane to the matter under consideration. Sir, if things have happened in the other provinces of this Dominion as they have in the province of Prince Edward Island-occurrences with which 1 am personally acquainted-substantial proof is afforded of the statement made by Professor Shortt and by the hon. member for Guysborough this afternoon that enormous increases have taken place in the number of appointments to the Civil Service. In the Department of Public Works in the province of Prince Edward Island, under the Conservative Administration, one man was removed from office and four men were appointed to take his place. Under the late Administration there were three men in the office of the Public Works Department at Charlottetown. There

are now six men in that office, and the names of seven men on the pay roll. Charlottetown is an old established community; there is no more work going on now than there was some years ago.
I am afraid my hon. friend is mistaken in the statement which he has made; I think he had better revise it.

I am quite sure that 1 am not mistaken. The circumstances under which this removal was made are decidedly objectionable. Shortly after the change of government took place some persons in that province who were connected with the Public Works Department and others who expected to be connected with the department, approached the resident engineer and boldly demanded from him a rake-off on the expenditure. The engineer was surprised, and refused absolutely to countenance such a thing. Pressure was brought to bear upon him; other men were brought to his office to influence him, but he stood firm and refused to be influenced. They told him that they would get square with him. The resident engineer at that time was superintendent of dredging for the province. The captain of dredge No. 9 was removed and a new captain was appointed in his place. The new captain, without any authorization or instructions from the resident engineer, proceeded to do dredging for private parties without making any return. When the resident engineer heard of this, he called the captain to account and reprimanded him severely. Upon being asked what authority he had for doing this dredging, the captain said he had been instructed to do it by the persons who were responsible for his appointment. These persons were called in, and the engineer was threatened with dismissal if he interfered with the captain of the dredge. Was he dismissed? No, but he was removed-superannuated.	The man
who was trying to protect the Government and the people of Canada, although he was well qualified physically and mentally to do his work, was superannuated at $2,800 a year and other men were appointed to do his work. I brought this matter to the attention of the Minister of Public Works some years ago. He told me that he would have an investigation made, and that if he found the charges made to be correct, he would dismiss every man connected with the matter.
No investigation has been held and no

removals have been made except the removal of the one man who was trying to protect the department. Now, Sir, if things like that are happening in the other provinces of this Dominion, we have an explanation of the enormous expenditure that has taken place under this Government, and of the enormous increase in the number of public servants drawing pay from the people of Canada. These are statements that cannot be controverted, facts that have come within my own knowledge, and they are but an index of what is going on all over Canada. This debate has taken a turn this . evening that led me to believe that I would be only discharging my duty by bringing this matter to the attention of the House 'and by publishing it, because I feel satisfied that what has been done in my province is but a small thing compared with what is going on in the other provinces, where great public works are in progress.
Mr. A. De WITT FOSTER (Kings, N.S.):
I do not intend to delay the House at any great length, but I wish to say a word or two, as is my inalienable right as a member of this House, on the subject which has engaged our attention since early to-day. I was much interested in listening to the debate, particularly that phase of it which has dealt with the so-called political truce said to exist throughout the length and breadth of Canada, and with the proclaiming of that truce. Hon. gentlemen are no doubt fully seized of the fact that when the wal broke out on August 4 and the political position of one of the great parties in this country was somewhat in danger, the first thing that was announced in the press was the so-called party truce. I wish to tell the House in what manner this so-called party truce was observed in the county from which I come, by hon. gentlemen opposite. No addresses were delivered in that county by myself on political topics. I did address a meeting or two upon patriotic lines, and I addressed a series of meetings in the county to	stimulate	recruiting, asI conceived that to	be the	most
important duty of any member of Parliament, after the great crisis which came like a bolt from the blue on August 4, and plunged this country, in common with the British Empire, into the greatest war the world has ever known. I had announced a meeting in my constituency on a certain evening, when I saw a poster announcing a public meeting to be addressed by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), by the member of the Local Legislature for

Kentville (Mr. H. H. Wiokwire), and by Sir Frederick Borden, the ex-member for Kings county. It was the annual meeting, at which the routine business of the Libera] party was carried on during the afternoon, and in the evening a public meeting was called, which was attended by a great many Conservatives of the town of Kentville and of the neighbouring country. They went to hear my good friend the hon. member for Pictou. I am bound to say that the hon. member for Pictou, in some parts of his speech, as he often does in this House, acquitted himself very creditably indeed. But, Sir, there was not one word said to stimulate recruiting in that county. The greater part of the speech of the hon. member for Pictou was an attack upon the Government, and upoh the Prime Minister, and upon the hon. the Minister of Militia particularly, for not having replied to that statement in the Globe demanding that the Prime Minister and his followers accede to the request of the Liberal party, to say that no election would be held till after the war. The ex-member for the county, Sir Frederick Borden, said that the Prime Minister of this country was prostituting the honour of this country by refusing to say that a certain number of sessions would be held before the Government went to the country. Prostituting the honour of the country, Sir, when the right hon. gentleman was engaged, to my own certain knowledge, in eighteen or twenty hours' work a day in the interests of Canada and of the Empire. The references to the Minister of Militia at that time were along the same lines. The execrations of Heaven or of some other place were called down upon the Government for the manner in which they were conducting the affairs of the country. The hon. member for Kings county for the Local Legislature even went into the realm of scandal upon that occasion, he even went on to tell the people that if the lid were taken off, the scandals would smell to Heaven, a beautiful thing to happen in a county where we were endeavouring to raise, as we since have raised, some two or three hundred men to go to the front. Yet hon. gentlemen talk about a truce being declared and having been violated by gentlemen on this side of the House. I was convinced from the start, as the youngest member in this House, that a truce was declared because it was politically advantageous to the Opposition party declaring that truce, and the minute it became known, and they realized that such a truce would no longer be ad-431
vantageous, then that truce would be broken. What of the detectives that it was said in the county were being stationed at Val-cartier and throughout the country to watch the Government, to watch the details of this, that, and the other thing? This was keeping the truce!
In regard to the matter of recruiting, I think it was in my own hearing that the right hon. the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), speaking in this House, said that if war broke out, in the interests-of this Empire, he would stump the urovince of Quebec, so interested was he that Canada should do her part. I would ask how many meetings the right hon. gentleman has held in the province of Quebec to stimulate recruiting there? He has held one or two that I have heard about. I would like to ask - how many recruits have been enrolled as a result of these meetings.
After the Liberal meeting of which I have spoken in my own county, I had a series of meetings at which I devoted about ten or fifteen minutes to answering charges levelled at the Government and myself at the meeting referred to, and for the remaining hour or two hours I did the best I could, as I have given of the best energy that was in me since the outbreak of war, in aid of this country and of the Empire.
Just a word or two with regard to Professor Shortt, a gentleman with whom I have but a very slight acquaintance. I am informed and have been led to believe that appointments to the inside Civil Service are based upon the results of '\ompeti-tive examinations. I know something about examinations, and the type of examination which has been set aiong a certain line, and I am bound to say that from my perusal of the type of questions that have been set at different times by the Civil Service Commission, a very great deal of fault might be found with the Commission itself; because in my humble judgment in some cases it is almost impossible to obtain the right man for efficient work so long as his appointment is to depend upon the results of the competitive examination set from time to time by the Commission under Professor Shortt. On one occasion, just a short time ago, the Civil Service Commissioin advertised for a technical man, a university graduate, a draughtsman to be utilized in the Department of the Interior, a man with special qualifications. A young man in my own riding spoke to me about the matter and I said to him, as I have said to all applicants who have spoken to me about positions, whether

large or small: There is the examination. There are the conditions laid down by the Civil Service Commission .and by the Government. When you have fulfilled those *conditions, when you have passed your examination and submitted your record, I will endeavour to see, if I can, that you get a fair show. That is all I will do for you or for anybody else. With regard to cajoling or pleading with any Civil Service Commissioner I should not deem it dignified in any respect for a member of Parliament to resort to that kind of procedure.
What I meant, Sir, by saying that I would endeavour to see that he got a fair show was simply this: If I could find out that Professor Shortt was keeping the position open for a graduate of McGill University or of Queen's University or of Dal-housie University or of . Acadia University or of any other university in the country, I should think it my duty to bring it to the attention of this House and of the country. In regard to the particular case I was speaking of just now, a gentleman in my own riding applied for a position as draughtsman in the Department of the Interior. He is a graduate in Arts of the university from which I come, and has had a two years' course in draughtsmanship and science at the same university. Later on he went to Montreal, where he spent four years graduating in both branches of science. He is an expert draughtsman. At the age of eighteen he. draughted his own plans, and built absolutely by himself an engine for his motor boat. He built the boat while going through college and sold it for $750, thus enabling him to pay most of his way through his arts course. He is a genius; a. man who, I dare venture to assert, is not equalled in his varied qualifications by any gentleman occupying a position in the inside service of this country. He took the examinations prescribed, whatever they were, and in due course gave my name to the Civil Service Commission as one to whom they might apply for a certificate of character. I had known him for six or eight years, and I filled in the ordinary form provided for that purpose. The young man came to Ottawa and was put to work in the Department of the Interior by the Civil Service Commission. Professor Shortt was at that time abroad, whether on Government business or his own I do not know, and I shall therefore impute no motives. But directly Professor Shortt landed in the city of Ottawa the first thing he did was to dismiss this gentleman from the service. I sent

him a courteous letter asking for the reasons for this man's dismissal. If the reasons had been that his work was not satisfactory to the department, all well and good; but the answer I got from Professor Shortt was that he had so many applicants whose qualifications were considered better than this young gentleman's that he had to dismiss him and appoint somebody else in his place whose qualifications were higher. I say he had no one whose qualifications were better than those of the young man to whom I refer, and I challenge any one, whether inside or out of this House, to give me the name of a candidate for that position and to state ihis qualifications alongside those of the gentleman to whom I refer. The proof of that is the fact that although this position was required to be filled in October -last, that position for which a man is urgently desired is still vacant. The young man I refer, to was dismissed after a month's work in the department. I was informed only yesterday that a new notice had been sent out asking for applicants for the same position. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, whether Professor Shortt was keeping that position open for some one from Queen's University or from some other part of the country ? What were the reasons why he did not allow that man to keep that position which he had filled to the advantage of the country and with the commendation of all those with whom he was working? I agree with what has been said by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, that Professor Shortt has too many things to do. Speaking at public forums and travelling back and forth throughout the length and breadth of this country, he is far too busy a man to devote his time and attention to the important business of conducting the Civil Service of this country, and he should forthwith be relieved of the duties of Civil Service Commissioner, and given ample opportunity to indulge himself along other lines which he seems to find more congenial.

I had not intended to intrude in this debate, which I am sure in the judgment of hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House has run to a point where not much profit is to be gathered from the discussion. I would not have risen 'were it not for the fact that my hon. friend (Mr. A. De Witt Foster) has made a reference to myself which I think calls for some reply. Just a "word or two in regard

to all this talk about political truce. What are the facts ? We might as well have them told fairly and squarely. Every one knows, at least every one on this side of the House and the Liberal party throughout the country, that when war came on the right hon. gentleman who leads us to-day as he has led us during so many years and whom we are so proud to follow, announced that so far as hue and the Lioeral party were concerned he did not propose to engage in political discussion, or to attack the Government's record in the ordinary public affairs of this country. Everybody knows he has kept his word, and that the right hon. gentleman has not appeared on any platform since the war began, except to ask the sons of his own race in the province of Quebec to come forth and follow the flag of old England. Everybody knows that a conference took place between the leaders of the two political parties in regard to the vacant seats in this House. Every one knows that an understanding was arrived at between them, that the men who should fill those vacant seats in this session of Parliament should be men of the same political stripe as those who formerly occupied those seats. And then Parliament met. So far as hon. gentlemen on this side of the House are concerned, so far as any agreement or truce between the political parties is concerned, everyone knows that there has been no such agreement between the political leaders in this country. X say on behalf of the Ihberal party in this country, that from the time the war began those who know something about what party management is like in this country, know that we have refrained from political partisanship and from attacks on the Conservative party in this country, in regard to the war or the expenditure for the war. That is where the party stands at this moment, while we claim the right in Parliament to perform our proper functions as an opposition in regard to other matters. But if the right hon. the Prime Minister and the men who sit with him think it is wise to go to the people of this country and ask for a verdict, the responsibility rests entirely with them.
And now I come to the matter to which my hon. friend from Kings (Mr. Foster) has referred. The only occasion upon which I appeared on any political platform since the war began was when I appeared with my hon. friend Sir Frederick Borden, a man who is beloved by the Liberal party of this country, a man who can
count as friends many hon. gentlemen who sit upon the other side of the House and who regard him as a man of great ability and one who has filled a high place during his long career as the representative in Parliament of Kings county. It would be well for this gentleman who succeeds him if, in the days to come, he could point to a record of achievement in friendships comparable in any measurable degree with that of which Sir Frederick Borden can boast to-day. I went to the meeting of the Liberal Association of Kings county. I did not attend the political organization meeting in the afternoon but I went to the meeting in the evening with Sir Frederick Borden. Did we make any partisan addresses, or arraign this Government upon their record, or discuss their political doings? Not at all, Sir. - On the contrary speaking for myself, I stated what I have stated here to-night in regard to the attitude of the Liberal party in reference to the Government of this country to that time in December and I said I did not propose to discuss party questions, and that I did not think that in the position which Canada occupied in the Empire and the position in which this Empire stood, engaged as it was in this great war, it was proper at all that we should have a political contest or that we should discuss political issues at that time. I pointed out what the consequences would be if you precipitated an election at that time and the reasons why it should not take place. I made no personal attacks upon any one. When my hon. friend undertakes to say that Sir. Frederick Borden attacked his own cousin in that county where they were both born, I say on behalf of that cousin as well ias on behalf of Sir Frederick Borden himself, that the hon. gentleman has not given a true version of what occurred at that time. Sir Frederick Borden discussed in a most dignified way, and from the standpoint of a public man who had occupied a high position in this country, the issues of war and the reasons why there should not be political discussion and a political contest. He spoke strongly, with all the knowledge that he possesses upon that question, and with that vigour which always characterizes his public utterances. When we think of Sir Frederick Borden we must always remember, when war's alarums come, when the sound of battle is heard throughout this land, that he gave his only son to the Empire, and the bones of his boy are lying on the veldt of South Africa to-day. His successor comes here with the story that we have heard to-

night about this distinguished public man to whom I have referred, and who is closely connected with my right hon. friend the Prime Minister by family and other ties. I would not have risen in this debate were it not to speak on behalf of my distinguished friend, Sir Frederick Borden, and in my own behalf in regard to the position which we took at this public meeting. From the time that it was apparent that \var was going to take place between England and the Allies and Germany, hon. gentlemen in this House and my friends throughout the province of Nova Scotia associated with me have not engaged in'political or partisan discussion. We have grounded our arms.
I think the suggestion made by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), who spoke immediately after dinner, was one which would be in the interests of this House to consider very carefully. What are the circumstances? We have Prof. Adam Shortt as chairman of a semi-judicial commission. Perhaps that is not a strictly correct description of his duties. However, he is chairman of that commission, and he stands in relation to the public service in very much the same position as a man occupying a judicial position. He cannot be removed from office except by a vote of Parliament. It is charged by these hon. gentlemen that he made a statement, which in the language of the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) was untrue and dishonourable, and a great many other adjectives and adverbs were used by the hon. gentleman which I need not repeat in regard to Prof. Shortt. As far as I am concerned, I do not know the gentleman and do not know anything about him. However, it would be much more dignified for this Government if they thought that Prof. Adam Shortt is a man with the qualifications and qualities which the Minister of Public Works declares he has, to come before Parliament and impeach him. What would be thought if we were discussing the decisions and the acts of a man occupying the position of chief justice of one of the provincial courts of this country in regard to a statement which he might have made upon any matter which for the moment might form the subject of political discussion, and it was thought necessary for every hon. member to denounce that chief justice in all the moods and tenses in which Prof. Shortt has been denounced to-night? Would not the appeal be at once met by the Minister of Justice, as a gentleman who had formerly

been on the bench, that high ground should be taken, and that the remedy which the law provided for those who have anything to say against a judge which would cause him to be impeached should be proceeded with in the regular way? In the history of this Parliament it will be found that on all occasions, if any hon. member sitting here in times past had any complaint to make of the conduct of any of the judges, the Minister of Justice and the Government took the ground that if there was any fault to be found it should take the form provided by law, that is, the form of an impeachment.
I am not going to go into the discussion of the question as to how many people were dismissed or how many people resigned or how many people were appointed in their places. I rose simply for the purpose of presenting the argument, and I appeal to the Prime Minister whether I am not absolutely right upon this question, that the proper course for the Minister of Public Works to take, if he has any complaint to make against Prof. Adam Shortt, is to make a motion in the proper way to impeach that gentleman before Parliament on account of the untruthful statement he is alleged to have made, or by reason of the fact that the qualities he is said to possess disentitle him further to occupy his office. If these gentlemen who have attacked him so viciously to-day have not the courage to proceed against Prof. Shortt by way of impeachment, then we have been simply listening to a lot of vapouring, and these denunciations will disappear before to-morrow's sun. I therefore submit that upon this question which has been brought before the House by the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, the Prime Minister is bound in duty, having regard to the statements that have been made by his colleagues, and the denunciations which have been put forth against Prof. Adam Shortt, to. take the suggestion of his own follower, the hon. member for Kingslon, and ask this House to proceed by way of impeachment against this gentleman. Otherwise, do not let us have the undignified proceeding of discussing these charges in this haphazard way about an official who stands in the same position, as far as Parliament is concerned, as would a chief justice of the court.
Mr. A. de WITT FOSTFR: Will the hon. gentleman deny that, speaking on the platform at the meeting at which I was present, and at which meeting I took notes, he accused the Prime Minister of making a hybrid alliance with the Nationalists, and

proceeded to arraign Mr. Pelletier, Mr. Blondin and Mr. Nantel, and said, among other things, that Mr. Blondin had to shoot holes through the British flag in order that he might breathe the air of freedom?

I have stated the
general tenor of my remarks upon that occasion. I state again that I made no partisan speech, that I did not anywhere discuss the political issues before the country, except as I have stated, and that I made no such speech as that to which my hon. friend referred.
Do you deny it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If there is no objection on the part of my hon. friends on the other side, I would like to make a few observations. Having moved that the House do go into Committee of Supply, I can only speak again by consent of the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I assume that the right hon. the leader of the Government has the unanimous consent of the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
With regard to what my hon. friend the member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has said just now, I would venture to remind him that sometimes hon. gentlemen opposite have not exhibited the qualities, upon which he has lavished such eulogiums, in making reference to persons occupying positions upon the judicial bench, because I have it very well in my recollection as appearing upon the pages of Hansard that the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition has publicly accused judges of his own province of Quebec of having made subscriptions to political funds in that province. If the right hon. gentleman had taken the course which my hon. friend for Pictou says should have been taken on this occasion, we would hardly have such charges appearing in Hansard.
The speech of Professor Shortt was made on the 15th day of January. My attention was directed to it shortly afterwards, and I thought it my duty to inquire into this allegation which was bound to convey a certain impression to the public that I did not think could be supported by the facts. I did not propose to take any action in the matter except by way of investigation, and placing before the members of this House and the people of the country precisely what were the actual facts. I sent to the House of Commons and asked to have a copy of the return-of which I know nothing whatever, as it had not been
brought to my attention, until I saw the observations of Professor Shortt as reported in the press. There was some delay in getting the return. It could not be found at first; but eventually I discovered that copies were being prepared, as I was informed, for my right hon. friend the leadc* of the Opposition.

Pardon me.
I never asked for that return until two days ago; I never saw it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am speaking
only of the information that came to me.
I was informed that copies were being prepared for my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. It may be that the statement made to me was not accurate.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am stating
precisely what I was informed, because I could not get the report when I first sent for it. The matter would have stood at that and would have been brought
11 p.m. to the attention of the House in the way I have just now suggested, except for the fact that the hon. member for the city of St. John (Mr. Pugsley) saw fit to endeavour to make use of it in the House for a partisan purpose. On the 25th of February, ten days after this statement had been made by Professor Shortt and before I had had an opportunity of investigating the facts, the hon. member (Mr. Pugsley) brought the matter up in the House for the purpose of making a partisan attack on the Government. I quote his language:
I have not that familiarity with the Civil Service that Professor Shortt, chairman of the Civil Service Commission, necessarily has.
That is a very true observation, and I pause here to bring to the attention of the House the fact that any statement of this character coming from Professor Shortt would be supposed to come from a man having special knowledge and authority to make the statement. That matter ought to be taken into account by hon. members and ought to have been taken into account by Professor Shortt before he made that statement. The hon. member for St. John continued:
He is a gentleman who is in the employ of the Government. He occupies, I presume, a quasi independent position as chairman of that commission; he has made the statement, made it publicly, made it with deliberation, that under this Government the appointments to the Civil Service in the lower grades are entirely a matter of patronage and he says that, whereas there have been something like 2,000

dismissals from the Civil Service, there have been some 10,000 appointments, making a difference of some 8,000.
He did not quote precisely the language of Professor Shortt as reported in the public press. Some consideration ought to be given to the fact that up to the present time Professor Shortt has not seen fit to modify or qualify in the slightest degree the statement reported in both the Ottawa papers that have been referred to. I quote in the Ottawa Citizen as follows:
Professor Shortt referred to a return brought down in Parliament a few days ago showing the names of 2,000 men who had been dism'ssed since the change of Government,
" Who," asked the speaker, " took the place of the 2,000?" The answer was, 10,000.
Is there any hon. gentleman opposite who will say that that did not convey to him the impression that this Government had dismissed 2,000 men and had appointed
10,000	men for i<be purpose of performing the same duties which had been previously discharged by the 2,000 men? I do not think any gentleman in this House or out of it will undertake to say that that is not the impression which would be conveyed to his mind by the language just quoted. I observe that later on in another newspaper . published in the city of Ottawa on the 26th day of February, which was quoted by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition, Professor Shortt alludes to this report of his speech. He also alludes to the discussion that had taken place in Parliament in regard to it, and he says he stands precisely by the report, nothing more and nothing less than the report. Possibly Professor Shortt did not see the report at all; he may have depended upon some statement in the public press as to what the report showed.
I venture to say that, if he undertook to quote from the report without having read it, he chose an unfortunate course. And if, having read that report, he made in public the statement credited to him in the press, then this action was still more unfortunate. I do not think that any hon. gentleman on either side of the House could in his heart and conscience come to any other conclusion about that statement than that which I have just indicated. I am not going to attribute motives to Professor Shortt in regard to this matter. If there is any hon. member who is ready now to suggest that Professor Shortt did not use the language attributed to him and that he would like to make an explanation about it,
I am perfectly willing to receive his ex-^ 
planation and to read it here in the House, in order that full justice may be done; or, if Professor Shortt desires an inquiry as to whether or not he used that language and denies that he ever used it, I would be perfectly willing to grant any inquiry that he might deem necessary for the purpose of justifying himself.
As his language has now remained unchallenged by him in any way, and as he did, as late as the 26th of February last, refer to the incident which took place in the House of Commons without seeking or desiring to modify in any way the report of his language on the 15th of February, I venture to conclude that there does not seem to be very much ground for any inquiry as to whether or not he did use the language attributed to him and which up to the present time has not been challenged by him.
Now, if I am to assume, as I think I am entitled under the circumstances to assume, that he did use that language, I venture to say that it was by no means a fair statement of the case and that it would be certain to convey an impression to the people of this country disadvantageous and unjust to the Government, and that without any warrant. I think I am within the reasonable judgment of every member of this House when I go that far at least. Prof. Shortt was speaking with special authority with respect to a matter that was supposed to be as much within his peculiar knowledge as within that of any man in Canada; and when he saw fit to ignore the fact that the very return which he had seen, or had not seen, contained over three thousand resignations, when he ignored the fact that a considerable number of civil servants had died during that period, that many had been superannuated, that others had left the service for other causes; when, ignoring all this, he saw fit to suggest that ten thousand had been appointed to do the work done previously by two thousand;-I desire in all moderation to say that I do not think his language could be characterized as quite fair to the Government of the day. If he desired to give statistics with respect to appointments and dismissals, he should have at least taken into consideration the elements to which I have just called attention. I think, if he had desired to put the case fairly before the people of this country, he should in all reason have taken also into consideration that in a country like this, a rapidly .growing and expanding country, there would probably be some need of additional appointments within

a period of three years.	But all
these considerations	were	absolutely
ignored by him.
I regret that the incident has been brought before the House and to the attention of the country by the methods which have been pursued. I would like to point out that when an hon. member on the other side undertakes to make partisan use of a statement which cannot be regarded as other than misleading, it is hardly to be expected that hon. gentlemen on this side will not resent it. It was promptly resented. My hon. friend for the city of St. John (Mr. Pugsley), following in the wake of the Liberal press of this country, by whom Prof. Sliortt's statement was used for the purpose of bringing an unjust charge against this Government, saw fit to bring that question up in the House, and it was resented on the spot. We have had this debate to-day in consequence. I think it would have been better if the question could have been dealt with in the method I had intended in the first place-that is, by placing before this House a plain and unvarnished statement of the facts, and an explanation, so far as any explanation is necessary, as to the increase in the public service of this country. If the question has been brought up, with the result that has been made apparent to-day, Mr. Shortt and every one else concerned have only to thank my hon. friend from St. John City and my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. We have nothing to apologize^ for in respect to the appointments made to the public service. Hon. gentlemen on the other side have spoken of their desire to debate the question. I tell them here and now that whenever they desire to debate that question we are ready to meet them, and I shall be most happy at any subsequent stage of the session to give them all the opportunity for that debate which they may desire by moving the House into Committee of Supply whenever they so wish. Whether they desire to debate it or to make a motion with regard to it, we shall be ready to meet them, and to combat any arguments they may bring forward. The debate has been more or less discursive, and I shall not now enter into some of the matters, more or less personal to myself, which have been alluded to, as this is not the time or the place for that. I will not compare honours as to changes of political opinions with my hon. friend for the City of St. John, as I have never claimed to be in his class in that regard.
I shall see to it that the returns are made complete with all necessary details up to
the present time. WTe shall have a return containing all the information that has been asked for, and some information, perhaps, that has not been asked for. We shall have that laid on the table of the House, placing all the information before my hon. friends on the other side, and we will invite them to bring forward any motion they desire on this subject of the appointments made to the public service.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (South Ren-trewl: I scarcely think I would have said anything in this discussion had it not been far two things: the remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. White)-the lecture, rather, that he proceeded to deliver to us on this side of the House-and the bland and childlike way in which my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) slid over his dismissals. He is an artist in a class all by himself. When he wants a man to resign or get out, he appoints him to some other position, perhaps some 200 miles distant at a smaller salary and without moving expenses.

The hon. gentleman
cannot name one instance.

Mr. Norris, of Chicago.
Look it up. If my information is correct, the hon. minister asked him to go to Prince Rupert.
I do not think the hon. gentleman's information is correct.

Wait until my hon.
friend hears what I have to say. My information is that a certain official who was in the employ of this Government in the city of Chicago at a fair salary was asked to go to a distant poin^, Prince Rupert, I think, at a smaller salary. This he refused to do, and he was decapitated by Order in Council. If my information is incorrect, I shall have to look up five or six other cases, but I give that to my hon. friend to think over for the night. In any case, outside of that altogether, the minister is an artist in his methods of decapitation. He spoke tonight of a time when I was Minister of Railways, and when we had so many men on the canals. The only extra men I think I ever put to work there were appointed upon the request of my hon. friend to have snow put on a certain bridge so that teams could get over in winter.

I do not think my hon.
friend wishes to misrepresent me. What I asked him to do at that time was to request the officials whom he was paying for looking after the bridge to put snow on the

bridge so that heavy loads would be able to cross. I did not ask him to put on any extra employees; the minister himself put them on to do work which could have been done by the men who were being paid to do it.

My hon. friend took
credit for it in his constituency.
I did not.

You cannot please some men, Mr. Speaker, whether you put snow on a bridge or whether you do not. Hon. gentlemen can understand that permanent employees are not engaged in running a swing bridge in winter; consequently we had to get men to put snow on the bridge in accordance with my hon. friend's request.
The hon. gentleman knows that the man who looks after the bridge is appointed by the year.

There was no man running the swing bridge in winter. But that is a small matter. My hon. friend the Minister of Customs, in the remarks which he made on this subject, did not show as much heat as the Minister of Marine did; he did not lecture us as did the Minister of Finance, and he did not do as well as the Minister of Railways, who did not say anything. He was a kind of happy medium, winking the other eye at the boys all the time.
I wish to refer for a moment to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. I have been in public life a good many years, and I have never made it a practice to display my loyalty by means of a brass band, nor do I find it incumbent upon me, in order to prove my own loyalty, to insinuate every time I stand up in this House that some other Canadian is not as loyal as I am. If that time should ever come, it would be the duty of the Government to have me interned until the war is over, because I would be either in favour of the enemy or not fit to be at large in this country. I hurl back into the teeth of the Minister of Finance of Canada his imputation of disloyalty on our part, and I tell him in the strongest terms that we on this side of the House are just as loyal as he or his friends. When it was said that we were disloyal, many years ago, he was one of us, and if we are disloyal, the Minister of Finance laid the foundation of that disloyalty, or was a party to it. We are not disloyal. The people of Canada from Prince Rupert and the Yukon across

to the Atlantic ocean are as patriotic and as loyal as any people in the British domains, England herself not excepted. I think the Minister of Finance rather forgot himself when he lectured us along that line. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) has shown whether or not he is loyal; he has a son with the Princess Patricias, fighting in France at this moment in defence of his country. That empty seat to my left, once occupied by the Hon. Dr. Beland, attests more forcibly than any words of the Finance Minister or of anybody else the loyalty of that son of French Canada. Another hon. gentleman, a French-Canadian member (Mr. Gauvreau), has a son defending the great Empire to which we belong. Is this a time, when we are asking men of all races and of all nationalities in this country to stand shoulder to shoulder in the fight for liberty, for a Minister of the Crown to stand up and fling across the floor of the House the taunt that we are not seized of the importance of the fact that Britain and her Allies are breaking their way through the Dardanelles?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not like to interrupt my hon. friend in the midst of the generous heat that he is developing in connection with this subject, but as a matter of privilege I desire to say that I made absolutely no charge whatever against the loyalty of hon. gentlemen opposite. When I referred to the fact that the war had inter-, fered with the trade and revenue of the country during the past year, hon. gentlemen opposite burst into laughter. I said that they did not appear to me to realize that the war was in progress, and that they had not a proper appreciation, in my judgment, of the scale-a proper sense of perspective in regard to the war; otherwise, in connection with the matter to which I was referring, they would not have treated it so lightly.
Why would we not have a proper conception of it ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
A proper sense of the scale or perspective, is what I said. If you will allow me, Mr. Speaker, as a matter of privilege, I desire to say that I have spoken on many occasions in this House and on many platforms throughout this country, and not only have I never impugned the loyalty of any member of the Canadian community, either Liberal or Conservative, but I have taken occasion to say on numerous occasions-and I reiterate the

assertion now-that I know of no disloyal citizen in the Dominion of Canada. I never made any such charge of disloyalty, and 1 desire my hon. friend to withdraw the assertion that he has made.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was referring only to the fact that in my judgment there was not an appreciation of the fact that t'he war was proceeding; that is all I said.

I do not want to impute motives, but I am afraid my hon. friend has let his talking apparatus run away with his better judgment. I do not propose, so far as I am concerned, to allow my best friend to impugn my loyalty, here or anywhere else.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has not been impugned.

My hon. friend, in his explanation, left out the very pith of what he said in the course of his speech. He turned to the hon. gentlemen behind him and, ironically speaking of something that the hon. member for the city of St. John (Mr. Pugsley) had said, he said that apparently we were not seized of the fact that at the present time the fleet of the Allies was breaking its way through the Dardanelles in an attempt to reach Constantinople. If that meant anything at all, it meant that we on this side of the House were looking at things in a small way and were not treating gravely the fact that our sons, our brothers and our fellow-countrymen are fighting in the trenches to defend our rights and liberties. If it meant anything, if it was intended to mean anything, it meant that.

What else could it
mean?

What could it mean but
that we were not seized of the gravity of the position in which our great Empire is at the present time. I want to say that we are seized of it, but is that any reason, because the Allies' fleet is breaking through the Dardanelles, that we should stand silent and let anybody break into the treasury of Canada?
Speaking of the truce, after consultation with the great leader of the Liberal party, several meetings that have been called were cancelled after the declaration of war. I have attended a good many patriotic meetings and addressed several-without a brass band or the accompanying reporter, but I have never discussed politics one way or the
other. I have read many red-hot political speeches of hon. gentlemen behind the Minister of Finance, who were cheering him a minute ago. I read some addresses delivered in Ottawa a few days ago, warm speeches. I do not object to them, I am not objecting to them, let them be made, because members of this House have a duty to perform. Sir, while this side of the House is ready to vote millions for the war, it is not ready to vote a dollar for graft. We are prepared to vote all the money that is necessary, as we did in August vote all the money that was necessary, to carry to a successful issue, the war in which the great interests of this country are involved, but we do not give up our right to criticise the administration of the affairs of this country. We are sworn as members of this House to do that. Shall we abrogate those functions, solely because somebody wants to dodge behind the fact that there is war? I say, Sir, that we ought to discuss, and the Government ought to invite discussion of these other questions; but their war appropriation can be put through without a word of carping criticism from this side of the House; but we are not going to be put in a false position.
Speaking of the truce, I am told that while in August we were voting $50,000,000 to carry on the war, pamphlets were being sent out from the city of Ottawa by the Conservative party under the frank of a prominent member behind the Finance Minister, whose name I shall give to the minister privately if he desires, attacking the Liberal party in the most bitter way. These pamphlets were sent back to me from the province of Ontario, having been sent out with the frank of an hon. member behind the Government, in August, w'hen we were here, Sir, nearly in tears, trying to stand shoulder to shoulder, without a whimper of partisanship and without an element of discord in our ranks on either side. Is that keeping the truce?
I want to go further, now that hon. members have brought the matter up. The member for Kings (Mr. Fowler) has accused my hon. friend from North Cape Breton of getting around to a certain point no matter where he started from. My hon. friend from Kings got around to Kings, his own constituency, within ten minutes. But the mountain laboured and brought forth a mouse, so far as partisanship in the Liberal monthly publication is concerned. I know something of what I say and what instruc-

tions were given to the Liberal monthly-publication from the time war was declared. The instructions were to give news and statements as to the conditions, but to make no party argument one way or the other- and it published part of the speech of the Prime Minister of Canada. And, Sir, all that the member for Kings could find was one small paragraph jogging the memory of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that we ought to get some of the war orders in Canada-and he lias acted along that line. He did not take it as any great or violent attack, he took it good-naturedly as ministers always do. It helped him, as a little criticism always does, to get a greater hustle on. That was all my friend could find. What can I find, if I look? Let me look for a moment, and discover what I find. I find a leaflet which has been sent to a friend of mine during the past few weeks, since we have been in this House, as being circulated in western Canada. Here is a leaflet sent out, published lby the Federal Press Agency, 47 Slater Street, Ottawa, Canada, Central publication and distribution office for the Conservative party of Canada. Here is one leaflet: "The aid which Laurier withheld from Britain was so much aid given to Germany." Here is a pamphlet, dated No. 6, 9-12, that would be the 12th day of the 9th month of 1914: "The vigorous and progressive western policy of the Borden Government." Party literature: Here is a good picture of the Prime Minister-no, it is not a very good one, I think I would have that one recalled. It is a worse one of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works. Really, what I cannot see about this western publication is why the Minister of the Interior's photograph was not inserted instead of that of the Minister of Public Works, as the Minister of the Interior looks after the lands of the West.
I find another one: "Liberals first advocated closure." This is an old pamphlet being circulated now, I suppose, as there was a greater stock on hand than there was demand for at the time. I come to another one, 14th of the 8th month, 1914, which I think would be August, ten days after war was declared. On the first page I find an insulting cartoon of my right hon. friend and leader which was sent broadcast through Canada: "Give credit to whom credit is due." This was sent out during the special session in August, after the outbreak of the war. I have another one: "The Liberals and the naval emergency: for the 
sake of a supposed party advantage they gambled with the future of the Empire." On the first page is another insulting cartoon of the right hon. leader of the Opposition. You say that was before the session in August. Was it? Listen to the first line of this pamphlet:
The war between Great Britain and Germany has come.
It must have been after the opening of war, after August 4th, and here is a pamphlet sent out by the Conservative party of Ottawa, a document of 30 pages, beginning with ridicule of my right hon. friend, at the very time that we were joining hands, willing to stand side by side, for the great Empire to which we all belong.
Let me give another one, prepared at an earlier date, which I am told was distributed after the August session. If my information is wrong I shall stand corrected :
The farce and the cost of the Liberal navy policy compared with the practical economical and effective policy of the Borden Government.
That has been distributed throughout the country during the last few months, I am informed. This is a pamphlet of eight pages printed and sent out by the Conservative party from their headquarters in the city of Ottawa. And my hon. friend from Kings talks about a truce !
Mr. A. De WITT FOSTER:	I did not
declare any truce.
My hon. friend did not have to, he was buying horses.
That is more than you did for the Empire.

I have another pamphlet here dated the 14th August:	"Relief for
the Western Settler." Talk about the war! Here is party literature being distributed through the West for party purposes, when we are supposed to have no parties. There is another one here called "Why the Three Dreadnoughts." This is a nice little booklet which reflects great credit on the printer, but it contains all the old line of attack on the Opposition. And here is a speech delivered by the right hon. R. L. Borden. I am not taking exception to that, for it was not very partisan; in fact, we helped to circulate it ourselves, we thought it so good. But if my hon. friends insist that that is breaking the truce we will have it recalled. Here is another one that has been circulated in Maple Creek, " The Borden Government the Homesteader's Friend." These are just a few of the pamphlets that are being sent out. Here is

one called: "Western Canada and the Liberals," which is being distributed very largely in the West. Then I Some to the Federal Press Bulletin, which hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House will know. As my hon. friend from Kings would say, it is a weekly eruption, spelled w-e-a-k-l-y. Hon. gentlemen surely cannot deny that this is being circulated. It bears the date December 24, 1914, and contains an attack on the Liberal party, also an insulting cartoon of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. Keeping the truce indeed! Keeping the truce and sending out tens of thousands of this kind of stuff. I have another Federal Press Bulletin here, dated January 7, 1915, almost down to the minute. And these gentlemen talk to us about violating the truce, which, so far as truce was made, we have absolutely kept. But we refuse to be tongue-tied in criticising what we think wrong. Take all the money you want for the war, but we are going to criticise the other things this Government does, and we are going to criticise them as much as we like. This Federal Press Bulletin contains a two-column article pointing out how futile the Laurier boats would have been in comparison with the dreadnoughts.
That are to be.

Two columns of that. Two columns of the most irritating partisan material that could be sent out. It points out that one party was practically against the Motherland. And this at a time when hon. gentlemen are saying, Truce, truce, don't hit us, don't criticise us, truce, there is a war on! And behind our backs they are sending out this party literature, giving us a stab in the back. The German nation has received the condemnation of the civilized world for having on several occasions fired on those bearing a flag of truce; but it is far worse for the people bearing the flag of truce to fire than to be fired on by others. Hon. gentlemen opposite say: You must not shoot, we are carrying a flag of truce. And at the same time they are circulating the most inflammable literature ever sent out by any party in the Dominion. My information may not be correct, but I am told that during the past few weeks thousands have been sent out from this city, and that about two thousand go out weekly. In the face of that, and after the speech of my hon. friend from Lambton (Mr J. E. Armstrong) on the navy, will hon. gentlemen opposite have the temerity to pretend that they are keeping anything that looks like a truce?
What was wrong with that speech?

It would have been an
elegant speech if it had been delivered in the heat of a campaign and when no war was on, or if the navy question was not a very live and debatable question _ between the parties. No man on this side of the House has discussed that question so far as I know, but it has been discussed by three speakers opposite as if to provoke a discussion on the great naval question, in order to get an excuse to appeal to the electorate. If hon. gentlemen opposite want to appeal to the electorate, let them do so. Do not do as you did in October, " stand shivering on the brink and fear to launch away." Make up your minds to go at it, if you want an'election. But so far as the war is concerned, we on this side of the House will give the Government no excuse for appealing to the country on the ground that we are not with them on every dollar desired for the war. '
Now I come to Professor Adam Shortt. There are more smiles now than when the ministers were speaking. Either the members of this' Government are very timorous and easily irritated, or else there was something in this thing that really annoyed them. I do not know which it is. The Prime Minister was the coolest of the lot, but even he just slipped a little near the end and showed a little warmth. Who is Professor Adam Shortt? Some hon. gentlemen who criticised him to-night showed the strength of their criticism by declaring that they had never met the man, or had had no acquaintance with him. If I might venture an opinion-and I will try to substantiate it-the trouble is not altogether over what Professor Shortt said, but because Professor Shortt has stood in the way of hon. gentlemen opposite driving a coach and four through the Civil Service Act. I am not saying that so much about the members of the Government, but I am judging by the speeches delivered by hon. gentlemen behind them. I except the Minister of Customs for this reason. The Minister of Customs declared Professor Shortt a great partisan. Now I have known Professor Shortt for many years, and I have never heard him utter a political syllable. I do not know to this day what the politics of Adam Shortt may be.
Oh.

I say that absolutely as a member of this House.
I
Who appointed him?

A Government that carried on the affairs of this country much better than their successors have done, a Government that introduced the Civil Service Act and lived up to it. But hon. gentlemen opposite are trying to poke their fingers through it. The reason why hon. gentlemen opposite are so sore against Professor Shortt is not because of what he said at the Forum, but because he has prevented them from getting their friends into office in violation of the Civil Service Act. The Minister of Customs dealt with his incapacity as a commissioner, and not to any very great extent, with what he said at the Forum. He read copies of examination papers, not to show what Professor Shortt had said at the Forum, but to show that he was not fit for his position. I think I am safe in saying that the Minister of Customs left the impression that the examination papers he read out to-night were for positions as packers, and that class of position.
I said clerkships.

We will look up Hansard to-morrow. My hon. friend mentioned the closing of boxes and that kind of thing. That is packers' work, and that does not require the examination for clerks which my hon. friend pretended was necessary.
It requires the examination for lockers, the preliminary examination, and they must pass that unless they are appointed preventive officers.
That is getting away from what I. am talking about; that is not the question. In the lower grades and in appointments such as that these examinations are not required.
That is not a fact.
Look at it and see if I am not right.
They are required to pass an examination.

They may be required to pass a very light examination, but my hon. friend^Jias many men in Ms employ in the lower grades who have not passed any of the examinations that were referred to in this House this afternoon. If my hon. friend will look up the requirements of the law he will find that they have a very high

standard, so high a standard that University men seek these positions in Great Britain, and they get a very high class of officials in this way. The intention of the Civil Service Act, which was not perfect, I admit, was to give the Civil Service a start in the right direction so that hereafter men of the highest type, men educated in our universities and collegiate institutes, might be drawn to the Civil Service.
Mr. A. De WITT FOSTER: They were turned down.

I am not going into details. My hon. friend was trying to get a man into the department. I know Dr. Adam Shortt, and I say, in the face of everything that hon. gentlemen have said, that there is no higher-minded type of man in the Dominion of Canada than Adam Shortt. He has his peculiarities, as the Minister of Public Works and I have our peculiarities, but he is the soul of honour, and there is ho higher type than Adam Shortt. I wish he were in the House to-night to reply to what some hon. gentlemen have said. I would like to see him on the floor of this House ready to discuss the great questions of the country, and if he were hon. gentlemen would find him a foeman worthy of their steel. I know the difficulties that ministers have with the Civil Service Commission-nobody better. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) smiles; he knows what I mean. .1 have had my difficulties with Dr. Shortt, and I have told him that he was wrong time and again, but I never imputed wrong motives to Dr. Shortt, because I believe he is incapable of entertaining motives other than those of the highest kind. What he was doing at the Forum was criticising our whole Civil Service system, and if you will read what he said carefully you will find that he took a fling at both parties. Of course, the present Government was in- that was the difference-but we had been in for a long time, and he criticised the Civil Service when the late Government was in power. He criticised the system very severely, and it was the system that we left that Sir George Murray was secured to investigate. Dr. Shortt thought that we had not arrived at the right kind of a system, that our officers were not divided in the proper way, that our work was not systematized, and that the ministers had too much to do. Dr. Shortt has always been largely opposed to our present system and wanted it

changed. Whatever he said on that occasion was meant to give an example of what he thought was wrong in our present system, and I do not think that he ever had any desire to impugn the motives or criticise the actions of the present Government. I know him as well as any man in this House knows him. As it is, the fact as to the figures must remain whatever Dr. Shortt said or did not say. The figures presented by my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) to-day show a chasm, to use the words of the hon. Finance Minister (Mr. White) between the sum of the dis-missable, resignations, deaths and desertions-
No.
I think so-and the sum of the appointments equals about 11,000 people.
There were no deaths in the returns.

Well, leave out the
deaths. It is said that civil servants seldom die and never of their own accord resign.
I do not know whether that is true or not, but they seldom resign unless they are forced to. The people will be asking:	Is
the Government justified in adding these thousands to the expense of the country at a time when we have a deficit-the first deficit in many years? They may not be so particular as to what Dr. Shortt said or did not say. From the public standpoint I do say that when we have a man who has held important positions in one of the leading seats - of learning in the Dominion of Canada, in a seat of learning which stands amongst the highest-that is Queen's University at Kingston, and I am proud to have some little connection with that university-when we have a man who has sent pupils out all over the Dominion to carry on their lifework, and who have carried with them a high respect for Dr. Adam Shortt, when we have a man who is in such a position that he cannot be touched by the House of Commons, one who occupies the position almost of a judge, I think it is as little as the Government can do to appoint some body before whom Dr. Shortt can come and put his side of the case as against the abuse which has been hurled at him by some gentlemen behind and on the Government benches. That is only fair to the dignity of this House, fair to the responsibility of the Government, and fair to a man who, notwithstanding what has been said,
stands high and will continue to stand high in the estimation of the leading educationalists in the Dominion of Canada.
